questions.stem: A 64-year-old man presents with crushing substernal chest pain radiating to the left arm for 40 minutes. He is diaphoretic with a blood pressure of 164/98 mm Hg. The 12-lead ECG is shown. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?

image.alt: 12-lead ECG showing ST-segment elevation with an anterior infarct pattern
image.caption: 12-lead ECG demonstrating ST-segment elevation (STEMI) with anterior infarct pattern and anterior fascicular block
image.source: Wikimedia Commons – File:12 Lead EKG ST Elevation tracing color coded.jpg (public domain)

options.A: Administer fibrinolysis immediately, because primary PCI can be delivered within 120 minutes of the time fibrinolysis could have been given
options.B: Arrange immediate coronary angiography with follow-on primary PCI, because symptoms began within 12 hours and primary PCI can be delivered within 120 minutes of the time fibrinolysis could have been given
options.C: Give a single 300 mg dose of aspirin and observe with serial troponins before deciding on any reperfusion strategy
options.D: Start unfractionated heparin and delay invasive evaluation for 24 hours to allow the infarct to stabilise
options.E: Discharge with an outpatient exercise tolerance test, because the ECG changes are nonspecific

questions.explanation: The ECG shows anterior ST-segment elevation consistent with acute STEMI, and NICE NG185 recommends immediately assessing every patient with acute STEMI for reperfusion, offering coronary angiography with follow-on primary PCI as the preferred strategy when presentation is within 12 hours of symptom onset and PCI can be delivered within 120 minutes of the time fibrinolysis could have been given. Fibrinolysis is reserved for when that 120-minute window cannot be met. A 300 mg aspirin loading dose should also be given as soon as possible unless there is clear evidence of allergy.

questions.stem: A 72-year-old woman with newly diagnosed non-valvular atrial fibrillation has hypertension, type 2 diabetes, and a prior transient ischaemic attack. Her CHA2DS2-VASc score is 5. She has normal renal function and no history of bleeding. Which of the following is the most appropriate long-term antithrombotic strategy?

options.A: An oral anticoagulant, preferably a direct oral anticoagulant such as apixaban, because her stroke risk clearly exceeds the treatment threshold and DOACs are preferred over warfarin in non-valvular atrial fibrillation
options.B: Aspirin 75 mg daily alone, because antiplatelet therapy is sufficient at this level of stroke risk
options.C: No antithrombotic therapy, because a CHA2DS2-VASc score of at least 6 is required before anticoagulation is started
options.D: Dual antiplatelet therapy with aspirin and clopidogrel for stroke prevention
options.E: Left atrial appendage occlusion as first-line therapy before any trial of medication

questions.explanation: The 2023 ACC/AHA/ACCP/HRS atrial fibrillation guideline recommends oral anticoagulation for patients with a CHA2DS2-VASc score of 2 or more (men) or 3 or more (women), and this patient's score of 5 far exceeds the threshold. Direct oral anticoagulants are recommended in preference to warfarin for patients without a mechanical valve or moderate-to-severe mitral stenosis. Aspirin is not recommended for stroke prevention in atrial fibrillation.

questions.stem: A 55-year-old woman with rheumatic moderate-to-severe mitral stenosis develops paroxysmal atrial fibrillation. She has no mechanical valve and no prior stroke. Which of the following is the most appropriate long-term anticoagulation strategy?

options.A: Apixaban, because direct oral anticoagulants are superior to warfarin in all forms of atrial fibrillation
options.B: Aspirin and clopidogrel, because she has no history of stroke
options.C: Warfarin (vitamin K antagonist), because direct oral anticoagulants are not recommended for atrial fibrillation associated with rheumatic mitral stenosis
options.D: No anticoagulation until atrial fibrillation becomes persistent
options.E: Reduced-dose rivaroxaban with routine anti-Xa level monitoring

questions.explanation: The 2020 ACC/AHA valvular heart disease guideline recommends vitamin K antagonist therapy for patients with atrial fibrillation and rheumatic mitral stenosis, and direct oral anticoagulants are not recommended for this population or for mechanical prosthetic valves. Anticoagulation should begin as soon as atrial fibrillation is documented, regardless of whether it is paroxysmal or persistent. DOAC trials specifically excluded patients with rheumatic mitral stenosis.

questions.stem: All of the following statements about antiplatelet therapy in patients with acute coronary syndrome are true EXCEPT:

options.A: A single 300 mg loading dose of aspirin should be offered as soon as possible unless there is clear evidence of allergy
options.B: Dual antiplatelet therapy should generally be continued for up to 12 months after myocardial infarction unless contraindicated
options.C: In acute STEMI patients undergoing primary PCI who are not taking an oral anticoagulant, prasugrel is offered as part of dual antiplatelet therapy with aspirin
options.D: De-escalation of dual antiplatelet therapy to aspirin monotherapy during the first 30 days is a routine, recommended strategy in all ACS patients
options.E: Ticagrelor with aspirin for up to 3 years is an option after myocardial infarction for high-risk patients more than 12 months post-MI

questions.explanation: The 2023 ESC acute coronary syndromes guideline explicitly states that de-escalation of dual antiplatelet therapy to monotherapy is not recommended during the first 30 days, so routine early de-escalation in all ACS patients is false. The other statements are supported by NICE NG185: a 300 mg aspirin loading dose, DAPT for up to 12 months, prasugrel with aspirin for primary PCI in patients not on an oral anticoagulant, and ticagrelor plus aspirin for up to 3 years in high-risk patients beyond 12 months. In patients already on an oral anticoagulant, clopidogrel is used instead of prasugrel or ticagrelor.

questions.stem: A 58-year-old man with heart failure with reduced ejection fraction (LVEF 25%) and type 2 diabetes is being started on guideline-directed medical therapy. He takes no renin-angiotensin system inhibitor, beta-blocker, or mineralocorticoid receptor antagonist. Which of the following is the recommended first-line approach for blocking the renin-angiotensin system?

options.A: Initiate an ACE inhibitor alone in all patients, adding an ARB only if cough develops
options.B: Initiate sacubitril/valsartan (an angiotensin receptor-neprilysin inhibitor) in place of an ACE inhibitor or ARB as first-line therapy
options.C: Start an ARB together with an ACE inhibitor simultaneously for dual renin-angiotensin system blockade
options.D: Begin hydralazine and isosorbide dinitrate instead of a renin-angiotensin system inhibitor

questions.explanation: The 2022 AHA/ACC/HFSA heart failure guideline gives a Class 1 recommendation to ARNI therapy with sacubitril/valsartan in place of an ACE inhibitor or ARB as first-line therapy for heart failure with reduced ejection fraction. Concurrent use of an ACE inhibitor and an ARB is not recommended, and hydralazine/isosorbide dinitrate is not a renin-angiotensin system inhibitor. Sacubitril/valsartan is therefore the correct first-line choice among the options.

references.title: 2022 AHA/ACC/HFSA Heart Failure Guideline: Key Perspectives

questions.stem: A 62-year-old man with heart failure with reduced ejection fraction (LVEF 30%) remains symptomatic on maximally tolerated lisinopril, carvedilol, and spironolactone. Which additional drug class now has a Class 1 recommendation to reduce cardiovascular death and heart failure hospitalization?

options.A: Intravenous iron supplementation for all patients with heart failure regardless of iron status
options.B: Ivabradine as the next step in every patient with reduced ejection fraction
options.C: Long-term digoxin to reduce mortality in heart failure with reduced ejection fraction
options.D: A sodium-glucose cotransporter-2 inhibitor (dapagliflozin or empagliflozin)
options.E: Routine addition of a loop diuretic at a fixed mortality-reducing dose

questions.explanation: The 2022 AHA/ACC/HFSA guideline defines four foundational therapy classes for HFrEF - an ARNI (or ACE inhibitor/ARB), a beta-blocker, an MRA, and an SGLT2 inhibitor - each carrying a Class 1 recommendation, and SGLT2 inhibitors are used regardless of diabetes status. An SGLT2 inhibitor is therefore the appropriate addition after the patient is already on the other three pillars. Loop diuretics relieve congestion but are not mortality-reducing foundational therapy, and digoxin, ivabradine, and routine IV iron are not among the four foundational classes.

questions.stem: A 74-year-old woman with heart failure with preserved ejection fraction (LVEF 60%), type 2 diabetes, and chronic kidney disease remains congested on a loop diuretic. Which of the following drug classes received a Class 2a ('may be beneficial') recommendation in the 2022 AHA/ACC/HFSA guideline for patients with HFpEF?

options.A: Sacubitril/valsartan
options.B: Spironolactone
options.C: Isosorbide dinitrate combined with hydralazine
options.D: Ivabradine
options.E: A sodium-glucose cotransporter-2 inhibitor (empagliflozin or dapagliflozin)

questions.explanation: In the 2022 AHA/ACC/HFSA guideline, SGLT2 inhibitors (empagliflozin or dapagliflozin) received a Class 2a recommendation for HFpEF to reduce heart failure hospitalization, and this benefit is seen both with and without diabetes. The other neurohormonal agents listed were not recommended at the Class 2a level for HFpEF in this guideline. Diuretics remain the mainstay for symptom relief of congestion.

questions.stem: A 52-year-old man has an average office blood pressure of 158/96 mm Hg on three separate readings, no target-organ damage, and no known cardiovascular disease. Lifestyle measures are being started. According to the 2025 ACC/AHA hypertension guideline, what is the recommended initial drug therapy strategy?

options.A: Begin a single low-dose thiazide diuretic and up-titrate monthly
options.B: Start one antihypertensive drug from any class and review after 12 weeks
options.C: Initiate two antihypertensive agents from different classes, preferably as a single-pill combination, alongside lifestyle changes
options.D: Admit to hospital for intravenous antihypertensive therapy

questions.explanation: The 2025 ACC/AHA hypertension guideline recommends initial treatment with two antihypertensive agents from different classes - preferably combined in a single pill - for stage 2 hypertension, together with lifestyle modification. The guideline retains a blood pressure goal below 130/80 mm Hg. Monotherapy is generally reserved for stage 1 hypertension, and hospital admission is not indicated without acute target-organ damage.

questions.stem: A 58-year-old man is found to have a blood pressure of 186/118 mm Hg on repeated measurement. He has no chest pain, dyspnoea, neurological deficit, visual change, or acute kidney injury, and the examination is otherwise normal. According to the 2025 ACC/AHA hypertension guideline, what is the most appropriate management?

options.A: Manage as an outpatient: intensify the oral antihypertensive regimen, confirm blood pressure with out-of-office measurements, and arrange close follow-up
options.B: Admit to hospital and begin an intravenous antihypertensive infusion immediately
options.C: Give sublingual nifedipine in the emergency department and discharge once the reading falls below 180/110 mm Hg
options.D: Administer emergency thrombolysis because of the severity of the reading
options.E: Start no treatment until ambulatory blood pressure monitoring confirms sustained hypertension

questions.explanation: A hypertensive crisis above 180/120 mm Hg in the absence of acute target-organ damage is managed as an outpatient with prompt adjustment of oral therapy and close follow-up, not with admission or parenteral therapy. Out-of-office confirmation with home or ambulatory monitoring is used to exclude white-coat effects, but treatment should be intensified rather than withheld in a patient with readings this severe.

questions.stem: A bystander finds a 45-year-old man in a restaurant who is responsive but unable to speak, cough, or breathe; he is clutching his throat. Which of the following is the recommended sequence of first aid for foreign-body airway obstruction in the 2025 resuscitation guidelines?

options.A: Begin with 5 chest thrusts, then reassess before any back blows
options.B: Alternating cycles of 5 back blows and 5 abdominal thrusts, starting with back blows
options.C: Perform a blind finger sweep of the mouth followed by 5 abdominal thrusts
options.D: Begin with 5 rescue breaths and continue with abdominal thrusts only
options.E: Start with 30 chest compressions as in cardiac arrest, then open the airway

questions.explanation: The 2025 American Heart Association guidelines recommend alternating cycles of 5 back blows and 5 abdominal thrusts for choking in both adults and children, always beginning with back blows. Options A, C, D, and E do not reflect this recommended sequence. Early activation of emergency medical services alongside these manoeuvres remains part of the choking response.

questions.stem: A 60-year-old man presents with crushing chest pain of 20 minutes' duration and a suspected acute coronary syndrome. He has no known allergy to aspirin. Which of the following initial actions is correct?

options.A: Give a single loading dose of 300 mg aspirin as soon as possible
options.B: Give 75 mg aspirin once daily as the only antiplatelet measure before hospital arrival
options.C: Administer routine supplemental oxygen to every patient regardless of oxygen saturation
options.D: Use the response to glyceryl trinitrate to confirm or exclude the diagnosis

questions.explanation: NICE CG95 recommends offering a single 300 mg aspirin loading dose as soon as possible in suspected ACS unless there is clear evidence of allergy; other antiplatelet agents should only be given in hospital. Routine oxygen is not administered: it is reserved for patients with saturation below 94% (target 94-98%), or 88-92% in those at risk of hypercapnic respiratory failure. A response to glyceryl trinitrate must not be used to make the diagnosis.

references.title: Recent-onset chest pain of suspected cardiac origin: assessment and diagnosis - Recommendations

questions.stem: A 67-year-old man with paroxysmal non-valvular atrial fibrillation on apixaban undergoes percutaneous coronary intervention with drug-eluting stenting for NSTEMI. He has normal renal function and moderate bleeding risk. Which of the following antithrombotic strategies is recommended for up to 12 months?

options.A: Aspirin, clopidogrel, and apixaban as full triple therapy for the entire 12 months
options.B: Stop apixaban and switch to dual antiplatelet therapy with aspirin and ticagrelor
options.C: Continue the oral anticoagulant with clopidogrel, and without prasugrel or ticagrelor, for up to 12 months
options.D: Warfarin bridging with aspirin monotherapy after 4 weeks
options.E: Clopidogrel alone for 12 months without any oral anticoagulant

questions.explanation: For patients with an ongoing indication for anticoagulation who have had PCI, NICE NG185 recommends continuing the anticoagulant with clopidogrel for up to 12 months, adjusting the DOAC dose according to bleeding, thromboembolic, and cardiovascular risk. Prasugrel and ticagrelor should not routinely be offered in combination with a needed anticoagulant because of bleeding risk, and long-term triple therapy significantly increases bleeding. Stopping anticoagulation entirely would leave the patient unprotected against AF-related stroke.

questions.stem: A 71-year-old woman is diagnosed with NSTEMI. After aspirin and antithrombin therapy, formal risk assessment (GRACE) estimates her predicted 6-month mortality at 4.5%. She has no contraindications to angiography such as active bleeding. According to NICE NG185, which is the most appropriate revascularisation strategy?

options.A: Immediate coronary angiography within 2 hours, because all NSTEMI patients require emergency PCI
options.B: Conservative management with no angiography, because her risk score is below 6%
options.C: Elective angiography at 6 months after maximal medical therapy
options.D: Consider coronary angiography, with follow-on PCI if indicated, within 72 hours of first admission
options.E: Refer for exercise stress testing before any invasive evaluation

questions.explanation: A predicted 6-month mortality above 3.0% places her in the intermediate-or-higher risk band, for which NG185 advises considering coronary angiography with follow-on PCI within 72 hours of first admission when there are no contraindications. Immediate angiography is reserved for patients whose clinical condition is unstable, and patients at low risk (3.0% or below) may be managed conservatively. A score of 4.5% does not mandate emergency intervention but does warrant early invasive evaluation.

references.title: Acute coronary syndromes - Recommendations

questions.stem: A 54-year-old man has an average office blood pressure of 146/88 mm Hg, no clinical cardiovascular disease or diabetes, and an estimated 10-year cardiovascular disease risk (PREVENT) of 9%. Lifestyle counselling has been provided. What does the 2025 ACC/AHA hypertension guideline recommend next?

options.A: Lifestyle changes only, with medication deferred unless blood pressure rises above 160/100 mm Hg
options.B: Immediate hospital admission for severe hypertension
options.C: Start high-intensity statin therapy only, without antihypertensive medication
options.D: Refer for a low-sodium diet programme and repeat office measurement in 24 months
options.E: Add antihypertensive pharmacotherapy to lifestyle changes, because the estimated 10-year cardiovascular risk is at or above the 7.5% threshold

questions.explanation: The 2025 ACC/AHA hypertension guideline uses the PREVENT risk equation and recommends offering blood pressure-lowering medication together with lifestyle therapy when stage 1 hypertension is accompanied by an estimated 10-year cardiovascular risk of 7.5% or greater in patients without clinical cardiovascular disease or diabetes. This patient's risk of 9% exceeds that threshold, so drugs should be added to lifestyle measures. The overall blood pressure goal remains below 130/80 mm Hg.

questions.stem: A 19-year-old university student with newly diagnosed asthma reports wheeze about twice a month and uses her reliever infrequently. Spirometry shows variable airflow obstruction. According to the NICE/BTS/SIGN asthma guideline NG245, which of the following prescribing principles applies?

options.A: Do not prescribe a short-acting beta-agonist reliever without concomitant inhaled corticosteroid, at any age
options.B: Offer a short-acting beta-agonist alone as needed, reserving inhaled corticosteroid for symptoms on most days
options.C: Start maintenance combination inhaler therapy with a long-acting beta-agonist in all patients at diagnosis
options.D: Offer oral corticosteroid therapy at diagnosis to prevent future exacerbations
options.E: Prescribe antibiotics for eosinophilic airway inflammation at presentation

questions.explanation: NG245 recommendation 1.6.3 states that a short-acting beta-agonist should not be prescribed without concomitant inhaled corticosteroid in any age group. Instead, as-needed low-dose inhaled corticosteroid and formoterol is offered as the reliever for newly diagnosed asthma in patients aged 12 and over (recommendation 1.7.1). Maintenance long-acting bronchodilator therapy without an inhaled corticosteroid and routine oral steroids at diagnosis are not recommended.

references.title: Asthma: diagnosis, monitoring and chronic asthma management (BTS, NICE, SIGN) - Recommendations

questions.stem: A 22-year-old man is newly diagnosed with asthma; he has symptoms twice weekly with no night waking, and spirometry confirms variable airflow obstruction. According to NG245, which reliever strategy should be offered to patients aged 12 and over with newly diagnosed asthma?

options.A: As-needed short-acting beta-agonist alone
options.B: As-needed short-acting beta-agonist plus as-needed low-dose inhaled corticosteroid taken separately
options.C: As-needed low-dose inhaled corticosteroid and formoterol as the reliever
options.D: As-needed long-acting muscarinic antagonist as the sole reliever
options.E: Regular oral montelukast as the reliever

questions.explanation: NG245 recommendation 1.7.1 advises offering as-needed low-dose inhaled corticosteroid and formoterol (the AIR approach) as the reliever for newly diagnosed asthma in people aged 12 and over. A short-acting beta-agonist alone must not be prescribed without an inhaled corticosteroid (recommendation 1.6.3). If symptoms remain highly symptomatic on this approach, low-dose maintenance and reliever therapy is offered instead (recommendation 1.7.2).

references.title: Asthma: diagnosis, monitoring and chronic asthma management (BTS, NICE, SIGN) - Recommendations

questions.stem: A 30-year-old woman has a 4-month history of cough and chest tightness with normal spirometry between episodes. According to NG245 (BTS/NICE/SIGN 2024), which single result in an adult would support a diagnosis of asthma alongside compatible symptoms?

options.A: Fractional exhaled nitric oxide of 25 ppb
options.B: Blood eosinophil count above the laboratory reference range, or FeNO of 50 ppb or more
options.C: Bronchodilator reversibility showing an FEV1 increase of 10% and 150 mL
options.D: A normal peak expiratory flow diary with no variability
options.E: Total serum IgE of 120 IU/mL

questions.explanation: For adults, NG245 recommendation 1.2.1 is to diagnose asthma if the blood eosinophil count is above the laboratory reference range or FeNO is 50 ppb or more, together with compatible symptoms. The guideline's bronchodilator reversibility threshold is an FEV1 increase of at least 12% and 200 mL (or at least 10% predicted), so option C does not meet it. FeNO of 25 ppb, a normal peak flow diary, and a normal-range IgE do not confirm the diagnosis.

questions.stem: A 66-year-old man with COPD presents with his first moderate exacerbation requiring systemic corticosteroids in the past year. According to the GOLD 2026 report, how many moderate or severe exacerbations place a patient in the highest-risk Group E?

options.A: None - all patients who smoke and have airflow limitation are automatically Group E
options.B: Two or more moderate exacerbations (or one hospitalisation), as in earlier GOLD reports
options.C: Three or more moderate exacerbations in any 12-month period
options.D: At least one moderate or severe exacerbation
options.E: Only patients hospitalised for a severe exacerbation qualify for Group E

questions.explanation: GOLD 2026 changed the Group E threshold to one or more moderate or severe exacerbations, replacing the previous definition of two or more moderate exacerbations or one hospitalisation. This patient with a single moderate exacerbation therefore now qualifies as Group E. GOLD 2026 also introduced a disease-activity assessment and an explicit distinction between initial and follow-up treatment.

questions.stem: A 63-year-old man with newly diagnosed COPD falls into Group E by exacerbation history. He has never used inhalers and has no clinical features of asthma. According to GOLD 2026, which statement best describes his initial pharmacological treatment?

options.A: Initial treatment should be a long-acting bronchodilator - a LABA or a LAMA - with escalation assessed at follow-up if needed
options.B: Initial treatment should be an ICS-containing regimen (LABA/ICS) regardless of asthma features, because exacerbations mandate early ICS
options.C: Initial treatment should be a short-acting beta-agonist used regularly every four hours
options.D: Initial treatment should be roflumilast combined with theophylline
options.E: No inhaler should be started until spirometry is repeated after 12 weeks

questions.explanation: GOLD 2026 introduces an explicit distinction between initial and follow-up treatment (new Figures 3.7-3.9): initial therapy for Group E patients without asthma features is a long-acting bronchodilator, a LABA or LAMA, with escalation decided at follow-up. Contemporary reviews of the GOLD 2026 approach also note that initiating LABA/ICS without asthma symptoms is discouraged, making option B inappropriate. Regular short-acting bronchodilator use alone is not a maintenance strategy for COPD.

questions.stem: A 70-year-old with severe COPD and chronic hypercapnia presents with an acute exacerbation and is given supplemental oxygen in the emergency department. Which oxygen saturation target should be aimed for until blood gas analysis is available?

options.A: 94% to 98%, as for all acutely ill adults
options.B: 100%, to maximise oxygen delivery
options.C: Below 80%, to avoid hyperoxia entirely

questions.explanation: Patients with COPD at risk of hypercapnic respiratory failure should have oxygen titrated to a target saturation of 88-92% until arterial blood gas analysis is available, as recommended by the BTS emergency oxygen guideline and NICE CG95. Most acutely ill adults instead have a target saturation of 94-98%. The aim is to avoid both hypoxaemia and worsening hypercapnia.

questions.stem: All of the following statements about emergency oxygen therapy in acutely ill adults are true EXCEPT:

options.A: Most acutely ill adults should have a target oxygen saturation of 94% to 98%
options.B: Oxygen saturation should be monitored with pulse oximetry as soon as possible
options.C: Patients at risk of hypercapnic respiratory failure should be targeted to 94% to 98% until blood gases are available
options.D: Supplemental oxygen should only be offered when saturation is below 94% in patients not at risk of hypercapnic respiratory failure, aiming for 94% to 98%
options.E: Patients with COPD at risk of hypercapnic respiratory failure should be targeted to 88% to 92% until blood gas analysis is available

questions.explanation: The correct target for patients at risk of hypercapnic respiratory failure is 88-92% (BTS emergency oxygen guideline; NICE CG95), so statement C is false - statement E is the accurate version of the same recommendation. The BTS guideline targets 94-98% for most acutely ill adults, and NICE CG95 advises monitoring saturation by pulse oximetry as soon as possible and offering supplemental oxygen only when saturation is below 94% (aiming 94-98%) in patients not at risk of hypercapnia.

questions.stem: A 44-year-old woman presents with pleuritic chest pain and breathlessness. Her heart rate is 98/min and blood pressure 124/78 mm Hg. The CT pulmonary angiogram is shown. If pulmonary embolism is confirmed and there is no contraindication to anticoagulation, which strategy should be started?

image.alt: CT pulmonary angiogram showing a large saddle embolus at the pulmonary artery bifurcation
image.caption: CTPA demonstrating a saddle pulmonary embolus filling the main pulmonary artery branches
image.source: Wikimedia Commons - File:Pulmonary embolism CTPA.JPEG (CC BY 2.0)

options.A: Aspirin monotherapy, because she is haemodynamically stable
options.B: A direct oral anticoagulant such as apixaban or rivaroxaban as first-line therapy
options.C: Systemic thrombolysis, because a saddle embolus always requires fibrinolysis
options.D: Inferior vena cava filter placement without anticoagulation
options.E: No treatment, with repeat imaging in 6 weeks

questions.explanation: NICE NG158 recommends apixaban or rivaroxaban as first-choice treatment for patients with confirmed pulmonary embolism, with anticoagulation continued for at least 3 months. Systemic thrombolysis with unfractionated heparin is reserved for patients with haemodynamic instability, and this patient is normotensive. Although the image shows a large saddle embolus, the decision to thrombolyse is driven by haemodynamic status rather than clot burden alone.

questions.stem: A 34-year-old man has a first episode of pulmonary embolism provoked by recent knee surgery. After initial treatment, the duration of anticoagulation is being decided. According to NICE NG158, what is the recommended minimum duration of anticoagulation for a first venous thromboembolism?

options.A: 2 weeks, because provoked events resolve quickly
options.B: 4 weeks only
options.C: 6 weeks for pulmonary embolism and no duration for deep vein thrombosis
options.D: Anticoagulation is not recommended beyond the acute phase for provoked events
options.E: At least 3 months

questions.explanation: NICE NG158 recommends treating a first deep vein thrombosis or pulmonary embolism with anticoagulation for at least 3 months, initially with a direct oral anticoagulant such as apixaban or rivaroxaban. After this minimum period, the decision to extend therapy is reassessed according to individual bleeding and recurrence risk. Fixed courses shorter than 3 months are not recommended for a first VTE.

questions.stem: A 61-year-old man with weight loss and progressive dyspnoea is found to have a large unilateral pleural effusion on the chest radiograph shown. Pleural aspiration is performed. Which result, using Light's criteria, would classify the fluid as an exudate?

image.alt: Chest radiograph showing a massive left-sided pleural effusion with opacification of the left hemithorax
image.caption: Chest X-ray demonstrating a massive left-sided pleural effusion
image.source: Wikimedia Commons - File:Massive Effusion2008.jpg (CC BY-SA 3.0, James Heilman, MD)

options.A: Pleural fluid protein divided by serum protein of 0.35
options.B: Pleural fluid LDH less than two-thirds of the upper limit of normal for serum LDH
options.C: Pleural fluid protein divided by serum protein greater than 0.5
options.D: Pleural fluid LDH of 100 IU/L with a serum LDH of 500 IU/L
options.E: Pleural fluid-serum protein ratio of 0.4 together with a pleural LDH at half the serum LDH

questions.explanation: Light's criteria classify a pleural effusion as an exudate if any one of the following is met: pleural fluid/serum protein greater than 0.5, pleural/serum LDH greater than 0.6, or pleural fluid LDH greater than 250 IU/L (about two-thirds the upper limit of normal). A pleural-to-serum protein ratio above 0.5 therefore meets the criterion for an exudate. Effusions meeting exudate criteria require further evaluation, including assessment for malignancy and infection.

references.title: Revisiting Light's criteria: a validated blood-free triple combination matches diagnostic accuracy in over 7000 patients

questions.stem: A 62-year-old man who smoked 1.5 packs per day for 25 years (37.5 pack-years) quit smoking 3 years ago and has no respiratory symptoms. According to the USPSTF lung cancer screening recommendation, which screening strategy is appropriate?

options.A: Annual chest radiography, because he quit within 5 years
options.B: Annual low-dose CT, because he is aged 50-80 with a 20 or more pack-year history and quit within the past 15 years
options.C: Sputum cytology every 6 months
options.D: No lung cancer screening at any age because he no longer smokes

questions.explanation: The USPSTF recommends annual screening for lung cancer with low-dose CT in adults aged 50 to 80 years who have a 20 pack-year or more smoking history and either currently smoke or have quit within the past 15 years (grade B). Because this patient quit 3 years ago and has a 37.5 pack-year history, he remains within the eligible window. He has not smoked for more than 15 years, so screening should not be discontinued on that basis.

references.title: Recommendation: Lung Cancer: Screening

questions.stem: A 29-year-old woman with asthma remains highly symptomatic - daily reliever use and weekly night waking - despite adherence to moderate-dose maintenance and reliever therapy, and her FeNO is 65 ppb. According to NG245, what is the recommended next step?

options.A: Refer the patient to a specialist in asthma for phenotypic assessment, including consideration of biologic therapy
options.B: Increase the short-acting beta-agonist reliever to use as often as needed
options.C: Start long-term maintenance oral corticosteroid therapy to control symptoms
options.D: Add a long-acting muscarinic antagonist without further review

questions.explanation: NG245 recommends referring patients whose asthma remains highly symptomatic on moderate-dose maintenance and reliever therapy, particularly with a raised FeNO or blood eosinophils suggesting an eosinophilic phenotype, to a specialist for assessment that includes consideration of biologic therapies. Simply escalating a short-acting beta-agonist reliever is not appropriate without an inhaled corticosteroid, and maintenance oral corticosteroids are not a guideline next step at this stage.

references.title: Asthma: diagnosis, monitoring and chronic asthma management (BTS, NICE, SIGN) - Recommendations

questions.topic: MASLD - assessment for advanced liver fibrosis with ELF
questions.stem: A 48-year-old man with metabolic dysfunction-associated steatotic liver disease (MASLD) and type 2 diabetes has an enhanced liver fibrosis (ELF) score of 9.8. Which statement best matches current NICE guidance?

options.A: Advanced liver fibrosis can be diagnosed from this ELF result alone and he should be referred to hepatology
options.B: He is unlikely to have advanced liver fibrosis, and reassessment for advanced liver fibrosis every 3 years in adults is sufficient
options.C: Routine liver blood tests should now be repeated every 6 months to monitor for fibrosis progression
options.D: The ELF test should be repeated every 2 years, the interval used for children and young people
options.E: Serum ELF testing should not be used in MASLD because transient elastography is mandatory first

questions.explanation: NICE NG49 recommends using the ELF test in people diagnosed with MASLD to test for advanced liver fibrosis, and defines advanced liver fibrosis as an ELF score of 10.51 or above together with MASLD (recommendation 1.3.4). People with an ELF score below 10.51 are told they are unlikely to have advanced liver fibrosis, and retesting every 3 years for adults (every 2 years for children and young people) is sufficient (recommendations 1.3.6 and 1.3.7). Routine liver blood tests must not be used to assess for advanced liver fibrosis in MASLD (recommendation 1.3.3).

references.title: MASLD: assessment and management - Assessment for advanced liver fibrosis in people with MASLD

questions.topic: Acute upper gastrointestinal bleeding - timing of endoscopy
questions.stem: A 66-year-old man is admitted with haematemesis and melaena and remains haemodynamically unstable (BP 80/50 mmHg, heart rate 130/min) despite initial resuscitation, with ongoing bleeding suspected. An endoscopic image obtained during upper gastrointestinal endoscopy is shown. According to NICE quality standard QS38, when should he receive endoscopy, and what lesion does the image show?

image.alt: Endoscopic photograph of a gastric lesion
image.caption: Endoscopic view obtained at upper gastrointestinal endoscopy
image.source: Wikimedia Commons — Gastric ulcer with visible vessel, endoscopic image (CC BY-SA 3.0, Jeremias)

options.A: Within 30 minutes of arrival, before resuscitation has been completed — the image shows a gastric ulcer with a visible vessel in its base
options.B: Within 2 hours of optimal resuscitation — the image shows actively bleeding oesophageal varices
options.C: Within 2 hours of optimal resuscitation — the image shows a gastric ulcer with a visible vessel in its base
options.D: Within 24 hours of admission — the image shows a gastric ulcer with a visible vessel in its base
options.E: Only after the patient has remained stable for 48 hours — the image shows a Dieulafoy lesion

questions.explanation: QS38 statement 2 states that people admitted with acute upper gastrointestinal bleeding who are haemodynamically unstable are given endoscopy within 2 hours of optimal resuscitation, whereas statement 3 applies the 24-hour window to haemodynamically stable patients. The image shows a gastric ulcer with a visible vessel in its base, not oesophageal varices or a Dieulafoy lesion, so only the option pairing that lesion with the 2-hour timing is correct. Ongoing haemodynamic instability therefore places this patient in the 2-hour group once optimal resuscitation has been achieved.

references.title: Acute upper gastrointestinal bleeding in adults - Quality statements

questions.stem: A 54-year-old man with cirrhosis is treated for acute oesophageal variceal bleeding with endoscopic variceal ligation and vasoactive therapy, and recovers. Which secondary prophylaxis regimen should he receive?

options.A: Combination of a non-selective beta-blocker (or carvedilol) and endoscopic variceal ligation as first-line therapy to prevent recurrent bleeding
options.B: A single additional banding session at discharge with no further endoscopy
options.C: Prophylactic antibiotics alone for 6 months
options.D: A non-selective beta-blocker with repeat endoscopy only after 12 months
options.E: TIPS is mandatory for every patient after variceal bleeding

questions.explanation: Baveno VII recommendation 7.8 states that first-line therapy for the prevention of recurrent variceal haemorrhage is the combination of traditional non-selective beta-blockers or carvedilol and endoscopic variceal ligation (A.1). TIPS is reserved as the treatment of choice for patients who rebleed despite this combination (recommendation 7.9), so it is not mandatory for everyone, and a single banding session or antibiotics alone (B and C) leaves the patient without guideline-directed secondary prophylaxis. Antibiotics are given from admission during the acute bleed (recommendation 6.7; NICE QS38 statement 6), and band ligation is used for acute oesophageal variceal bleeding (QS38 statement 7), but neither replaces combination secondary prophylaxis.

references.title: Baveno VII - Renewing consensus in portal hypertension
references.org: Journal of Hepatology / EASL Baveno VII Faculty

questions.topic: Severe active Crohn's disease - biologic therapy
questions.stem: A 30-year-old man has severe active Crohn's disease that has not responded to conventional therapy including corticosteroids and immunosuppression. He has no contraindication to biologic therapy. Which treatment does NICE recommend?

options.A: Infliximab may only be used after the patient has undergone intestinal resection
options.B: Biologic therapy is restricted to patients who are intolerant of azathioprine only
options.C: Infliximab and adalimumab, within their licensed indications, are recommended treatment options for adults with severe active Crohn's disease whose disease has not responded to conventional therapy
options.D: Methotrexate must be trialled for 12 months before any biologic is offered
options.E: Budesonide is the preferred step-up therapy at this stage

questions.explanation: NICE NG129 recommendation 1.2.12 states that infliximab and adalimumab, within their licensed indications, are recommended as treatment options for adults with severe active Crohn's disease whose disease has not responded to conventional therapy (including immunosuppressive and/or corticosteroid treatments), or who are intolerant of or have contraindications to conventional therapy. Infliximab or adalimumab is given as a planned course of treatment until treatment failure, including the need for surgery.

references.title: Crohn's disease: management - Recommendations

questions.topic: Hepatitis B in pregnancy - prevention of mother-to-child transmission
questions.stem: A 29-year-old HBsAg-positive woman attends at 28 weeks' gestation. Her HBV DNA is 350,000 IU/mL, she is HBeAg-negative and antiviral-naive. What does AASLD/IDSA recommend to prevent mother-to-child transmission?

options.A: No antiviral therapy, because she is HBeAg-negative
options.B: Start entecavir at gestational week 28
options.C: Initiate tenofovir disoproxil fumarate or tenofovir alafenamide at gestational week 28, with the infant given hepatitis B immune globulin and the first vaccine dose within 12 hours of birth
options.D: Defer antiviral therapy until after delivery and rely on infant vaccination alone
options.E: Start tenofovir at gestational week 16 irrespective of HBV DNA level

questions.explanation: For pregnant people with HBV DNA greater than 200,000 IU/mL at any time point during pregnancy, regardless of HBeAg status, AASLD recommends initiating tenofovir disoproxil fumarate or tenofovir alafenamide at gestational week 28 (strong recommendation, moderate certainty); tenofovir disoproxil fumarate has the more extensive safety record in pregnancy. Infants born to HBsAg-positive women should receive hepatitis B immune globulin and the first dose of HBV vaccine within 12 hours of birth. Starting at week 16 applies only when infant HBIG use is unavailable.

references.title: AASLD/IDSA Practice Guideline on Treatment of Chronic Hepatitis B

questions.stem: A treatment-naive adult with chronic hepatitis C genotype 3 infection has no cirrhosis, no prior hepatitis C treatment and no contraindications to therapy. According to the AASLD/IDSA simplified treatment guidance, which regimen and duration are recommended?

options.A: Glecaprevir/pibrentasvir once daily with food for 8 weeks
options.B: Glecaprevir/pibrentasvir for 12 weeks
options.C: Sofosbuvir/velpatasvir for 4 weeks
options.D: Ledipasvir/sofosbuvir for 12 weeks
options.E: Treatment should be deferred until fibrosis progresses to cirrhosis

questions.explanation: The simplified pathway applies to treatment-naive adults with chronic HCV of any genotype who do not have cirrhosis; genotyping is not required when a pangenotypic regimen is used. Recommended regimens are glecaprevir/pibrentasvir for 8 weeks (taken with food) or sofosbuvir/velpatasvir for 12 weeks. A 12-week glecaprevir/pibrentasvir course (B) is not the recommended duration for this treatment-naive non-cirrhotic patient, and neither sofosbuvir/velpatasvir for 4 weeks (C) nor ledipasvir/sofosbuvir (D) is a recommended regimen.

references.title: AASLD-IDSA HCV Guidance: Initial treatment of adults with HCV infection

questions.topic: Primary biliary cholangitis - ursodeoxycholic acid therapy
questions.stem: A 55-year-old woman is newly diagnosed with primary biliary cholangitis (AMA positive, ALP twice the upper limit of normal, normal bilirubin, compensated liver disease). Which statement is correct?

options.A: Ursodeoxycholic acid at 5-7 mg/kg/day is the recommended first-line dose
options.B: Ursodeoxycholic acid at 13-15 mg/kg/day is first-line, and biochemical response should be evaluated after 12 months of therapy
options.C: Obeticholic acid should be offered as first-line therapy in patients with decompensated cirrhosis (CTP class B or C)
options.D: Serial liver biopsy is required to judge treatment response
options.E: Ursodeoxycholic acid at 23-25 mg/kg/day produces better outcomes than 13-15 mg/kg/day

questions.explanation: The AASLD practice guidance states that ursodeoxycholic acid at a dose of 13 to 15 mg/kg/day is first-line therapy for PBC, and that studies showing improved survival have all used this dose; a dose comparison showed 13-15 mg/kg/day superior to both 5-7 and 23-25 mg/kg/day in biochemical response. Biochemical response is assessed after 12 months of therapy (used by the GLOBE and UK-PBC scores). The 2021 practice guidance update revises statements 9 and 10: fibrates are discouraged in patients with decompensated liver disease, and obeticholic acid is contraindicated in advanced cirrhosis (current or prior decompensation, such as encephalopathy or coagulopathy, or portal hypertension, such as ascites, varices or persistent thrombocytopenia).

references.title: Primary biliary cholangitis: AASLD Practice Guidance

questions.topic: Colorectal cancer screening - age and grade
questions.stem: A healthy 47-year-old adult with no symptoms and average risk asks about colorectal cancer screening. According to the US Preventive Services Task Force, what is the recommendation and its grade?

options.A: Screening is recommended with grade A, because grade A applies from age 45 onwards
options.B: Screening is not recommended before age 50
options.C: Screening is recommended with grade B for adults aged 45 to 49 years
options.D: Selective screening is offered with grade C for this age group
options.E: Grade B applies to ages 45 to 49 and grade A to ages 50 to 75, so no screening should be offered at 47

questions.explanation: The 2021 USPSTF recommendation states that clinicians should screen adults aged 45 to 49 years for colorectal cancer (grade B), and screen all adults aged 50 to 75 years (grade A). Adults aged 76 to 85 years should be selectively screened (grade C), considering overall health, prior screening history and patient preferences.

references.title: Colorectal Cancer: Screening

questions.stem: A 60-year-old man with cirrhosis and tense ascites develops acute kidney injury that meets criteria for hepatorenal syndrome-AKI (HRS-AKI) after diagnostic paracentesis and albumin challenge, with no improvement after diuretic withdrawal and volume expansion. Which is the treatment of choice?

options.A: Terlipressin given alone without albumin
options.B: Midodrine plus octreotide as first-line therapy
options.C: Immediate renal replacement therapy without a trial of medical therapy
options.D: Noradrenaline infusion in preference to terlipressin when terlipressin is available
options.E: Vasoconstrictor drugs in combination with albumin, with terlipressin as the preferred agent

questions.explanation: The AASLD practice guidance states that the treatment of choice for HRS-AKI is vasoconstrictor drugs in combination with albumin, and that the preferred drug is terlipressin, given either as IV bolus or continuous IV infusion. Where terlipressin is not available, noradrenaline should be given; if neither can be administered, oral midodrine with octreotide is used. Vasoconstrictors are maintained until creatinine returns to baseline, up to 14 days.

references.title: Diagnosis, Evaluation, and Management of Ascites, Spontaneous Bacterial Peritonitis and Hepatorenal Syndrome [updated August 2021]

questions.topic: Chronic kidney disease - blood pressure target
questions.stem: A 65-year-old man has CKD stage G3b with albuminuria A2 and treated hypertension, and tolerates his current regimen without postural symptoms. According to the KDIGO 2024 CKD guideline, what systolic blood pressure target is recommended when tolerated?

options.A: Below 120 mm Hg using standardized office blood pressure measurement
options.B: Below 130 mm Hg regardless of the measurement method used
options.C: Below 140 mm Hg
options.D: Below 120 mm Hg measured by home blood pressure monitoring
options.E: A systolic target of 160 mm Hg is acceptable in CKD

questions.explanation: KDIGO 2024 recommends treating adults with CKD and hypertension to a standardized office systolic blood pressure target below 120 mm Hg, when tolerated (2B). KDIGO advises considering less intensive blood pressure-lowering therapy in people with frailty, high risk of falls and fractures, very limited life expectancy, or symptomatic postural hypotension, so the intensive target is applied only when it is tolerated.

references.title: KDIGO 2024 Clinical Practice Guideline for the Management of Blood Pressure in Chronic Kidney Disease

questions.stem: A 67-year-old man develops acute kidney injury after prolonged hypovolaemia. His urine sediment is shown. Serum creatinine is 1.8 times baseline, and urine output has been 0.6 mL/kg/h for the last 8 hours. What is his KDIGO acute kidney injury stage, and what does the urine sediment indicate?

image.caption: Urine sediment examined under light microscopy
image.source: Wikimedia Commons — Granular casts in urine sediment, light microscopy (CC BY 4.0, Ajay Kumar Chaurasiya)

options.A: He does not have acute kidney injury
options.B: Stage 1; the granular casts shown indicate established intrinsic tubular injury rather than a pre-renal state
options.C: Stage 1; the hyaline casts shown indicate a pre-renal state
options.D: Stage 2, because urine output has been below 0.5 mL/kg/h for 12 hours or more
options.E: Stage 3, because renal replacement therapy must be started immediately

questions.explanation: KDIGO stage 1 is defined by a serum creatinine increase to 1.5-1.9 times baseline, an increase of at least 0.3 mg/dl (26.5 micromol/l), or urine output below 0.5 ml/kg/h for 6 to 12 hours; this patient meets the creatinine criterion (1.8 times baseline) but not the urine-output criterion, since his output is 0.6 ml/kg/h. Stage 2 requires 2.0-2.9 times baseline or urine output below 0.5 ml/kg/h for 12 hours or more, and stage 3 requires 3.0 times baseline or an increase to at least 4.0 mg/dl, initiation of renal replacement therapy, urine output below 0.3 ml/kg/h for 24 hours or more, or anuria for 12 hours or more. The sediment shown contains granular casts, which indicate established intrinsic (tubular) acute kidney injury rather than the hyaline casts expected in a purely pre-renal state.

references.title: KDIGO Clinical Practice Guideline for Acute Kidney Injury

questions.topic: CKD-mineral and bone disorder - phosphate management
questions.stem: A 58-year-old man on haemodialysis (CKD stage G5D) has a serum phosphate of 1.9 mmol/l (above the normal range) with a normal serum calcium. According to the KDIGO 2017 CKD-MBD guideline, how should this be managed?

options.A: Lower the elevated phosphate level toward the normal range
options.B: No phosphate intervention is needed in dialysis patients
options.C: Start treatment only if the serum calcium is elevated
options.D: Intervene only when a bone biopsy shows adynamic bone disease
options.E: Allow phosphate to rise until PTH exceeds 9 times the upper normal limit

questions.explanation: KDIGO 2017 recommends that in patients with CKD G3a-G5 serum phosphate should be maintained in the normal range, and in patients with CKD G5D elevated phosphate levels should be lowered toward the normal range (both 2C). The same guideline suggests avoiding hypercalcemia in adults with CKD G3a-G5D, and treatment is not deferred until calcium is elevated or until bone biopsy findings change.

references.title: KDIGO 2017 Clinical Practice Guideline Update for the Diagnosis, Evaluation, Prevention, and Treatment of Chronic Kidney Disease-Mineral and Bone Disorder (CKD-MBD)

questions.stem: A 62-year-old woman receiving maintenance haemodialysis has anaemia with haemoglobin 8.5 g/dl (85 g/l), no active bleeding and no contraindication to erythropoiesis-stimulating agents. According to the KDIGO 2026 anaemia in CKD guideline, when should ESA therapy be initiated?

options.A: Only when haemoglobin falls below 7.0 g/dl
options.B: When haemoglobin is below 12.0 g/dl to prevent cardiovascular events
options.C: At a haemoglobin of 8.0 g/dl or below in all stages of CKD
options.D: Haemoglobin should not guide initiation; wait until a red cell transfusion is required
options.E: When haemoglobin is at or below 9.0-10.0 g/dl (90-100 g/l) in people with CKD G5D receiving haemodialysis or peritoneal dialysis

questions.explanation: KDIGO 2026 recommendation 3.2.1 (2D) suggests initiating ESA therapy when haemoglobin is at or below 9.0-10.0 g/dl (90-100 g/l) in people with anaemia and CKD G5D receiving haemodialysis or peritoneal dialysis. During maintenance, the guideline recommends targeting haemoglobin below 11.5 g/dl (1D), and it advises against using ESAs and HIF-prolyl hydroxylase inhibitors in combination.

references.title: KDIGO 2026 Clinical Practice Guideline for the Management of Anemia in Chronic Kidney Disease

questions.stem: A 50-year-old man with nephrotic-range proteinuria has biopsy-proven membranous nephropathy, and renal vein thrombosis is demonstrated on imaging. Which management is indicated?

options.A: Antiplatelet therapy alone
options.B: Full anticoagulation
options.C: No anticoagulation, because membranous glomerulonephritis carries a low risk of thromboembolism
options.D: Prophylactic-dose anticoagulation only, without full-dose therapy

questions.explanation: KDIGO 2021 practice point 1.7.1 states that full anticoagulation is indicated for patients with thromboembolic events occurring in the context of nephrotic syndrome, while prophylactic anticoagulation should be employed when the risk of thromboembolism exceeds the estimated patient-specific risk of an anticoagulation-induced serious bleeding event. The guideline's anticoagulation figure notes that membranous glomerulonephritis carries a particularly high risk of thromboembolic events. This patient has a documented thromboembolic event, so full anticoagulation is required rather than prophylaxis alone.

references.title: KDIGO 2021 Clinical Practice Guideline for the Management of Glomerular Diseases

questions.stem: A patient is starting incident haemodialysis and the vascular access plan is being decided. According to the KDOQI vascular access guideline, which approach is recommended?

options.A: An arteriovenous access (AVF or AVG) in preference to a central venous catheter in most incident and prevalent haemodialysis patients
options.B: A central venous catheter as the first-choice access because of a lower infection risk
options.C: An arteriovenous fistula only; arteriovenous grafts should never be used
options.D: A tunnelled central venous catheter for the first 6 months in all patients

questions.explanation: KDOQI statement 2.3 (Conditional Recommendation, Low Quality of Evidence) suggests an arteriovenous access (AVF or AVG) in preference to a central venous catheter in most incident and prevalent haemodialysis patients, because of the lower infection risk associated with AV access use. The choice between AVF and AVG is based on the clinician's best clinical judgment, considering vessel characteristics, patient comorbidities, health circumstances and personal preferences.

references.title: KDOQI Clinical Practice Guideline for Vascular Access

questions.stem: A 70-year-old man in hospital has a serum potassium of 6.8 mmol/l with peaked T waves on ECG. According to the UK Kidney Association guideline, what is the appropriate immediate treatment?

options.A: Oral sodium zirconium cyclosilicate with reassessment in 24 hours
options.B: Nebulised salbutamol alone
options.C: Intravenous calcium for myocardial stabilisation, together with urgent potassium-lowering therapy such as a two-stage insulin-glucose regimen
options.D: Immediate haemodialysis in every case, before any medical measures
options.E: Calcium resonium 30 g per rectum as first-line acute therapy

questions.explanation: The UKKA guideline defines severe hyperkalaemia as potassium of 6.5 mmol/l or above, and uses intravenous calcium salts for patients with ECG changes to stabilise the myocardium. Potassium is then lowered urgently with a two-stage insulin-glucose regimen with post-treatment blood glucose monitoring; sodium zirconium cyclosilicate 10 g three times daily for up to 72 hours may be used in severe hyperkalaemia. Calcium resonium is no longer routinely recommended in the acute setting.

references.title: UKKA Clinical Practice Guideline - Management of Hyperkalaemia in Adults (updated July 2026)

questions.stem: In April 2025 the FDA granted accelerated approval to atrasentan (Vanrafia) for which indication?

options.A: Treatment of C3 glomerulopathy
options.B: Reducing proteinuria in primary IgA nephropathy when UPCR is at least 0.5 g/g
options.C: Proven slowing of kidney function decline in IgA nephropathy
options.D: Reducing proteinuria in adults with primary IgA nephropathy at risk of rapid disease progression, generally defined as UPCR of 1.5 g/g or more
options.E: Chronic kidney disease due to type 2 diabetes with UACR of 30 mg/g or more

questions.explanation: FDA granted accelerated approval on 2 April 2025 for Vanrafia (atrasentan) to reduce proteinuria in adults with primary immunoglobulin A nephropathy at risk of rapid disease progression, generally a urine protein-to-creatinine ratio of 1.5 g/g or more. Approval was based on proteinuria reduction in the ALIGN trial, and the label states that it has not been established whether Vanrafia slows kidney function decline; the recommended dose is 0.75 mg orally once daily.

questions.stem: A 35-year-old man presents with renal colic; an abdominal radiograph taken during the attack is shown. CT confirms a 6 mm distal ureteral stone with no infection and normal renal function, and he is consented to conservative/medical management. Which statement correctly describes the radiograph and the EAU guideline recommendation?

image.alt: Abdominal radiograph taken during renal colic
image.caption: Plain abdominal radiograph taken during the episode of renal colic
image.source: Wikimedia Commons — Kidney stones on abdominal X-ray (CC BY 2.0, Bill Rhodes)

options.A: The radiograph shows radiopaque calculi, and an alpha-blocker is only recommended for distal ureteral stones greater than 10 mm
options.B: The radiograph shows radiopaque calculi, and an alpha-blocker should be offered as medical expulsive therapy as one of the treatment options for a distal ureteral stone 5 to 10 mm in size
options.C: The radiograph shows bilateral staghorn calculi, and an alpha-blocker should be offered as medical expulsive therapy as one of the treatment options for a distal ureteral stone 5 to 10 mm in size
options.D: The radiograph shows radiolucent uric acid calculi, and immediate ureteroscopy is mandatory for every 6 mm stone

questions.explanation: The radiograph shows radiopaque (not radiolucent) calculi, and no staghorn calculus is present. The EAU urolithiasis guidelines give a strong-rated recommendation to offer alpha-blockers as medical expulsive therapy as one of the treatment options for distal ureteral stones 5 to 10 mm, with the footnote that alpha-blockers are an off-label treatment, and this patient's 6 mm distal stone falls within that range. Stones greater than 10 mm (A) fall outside the recommended size range for this option, and antibiotics are reserved for infected or high-risk cases rather than used routinely.

questions.stem: A 68-year-old man reports visible haematuria on two occasions. Urine culture is negative and there is no urinary tract infection. What does NICE NG12 recommend?

options.A: Suspected cancer pathway referral for bladder cancer, because he is aged 45 or over with unexplained visible haematuria without urinary tract infection
options.B: Watchful waiting with repeat urine testing after 6 months
options.C: Referral is only indicated if he is aged 60 or over with non-visible haematuria
options.D: Referral only if a CT urogram shows a filling defect

questions.explanation: NICE NG12 recommendation 1.6.4 advises a suspected cancer pathway referral for bladder cancer if the person is aged 45 or over and has unexplained visible haematuria without urinary tract infection, or visible haematuria that persists or recurs after successful treatment of a urinary tract infection. The alternative aged-60 criterion applies to unexplained non-visible haematuria together with dysuria or a raised white cell count, not to this patient.

questions.topic: Lower urinary tract symptoms - 5-alpha reductase inhibitor
questions.stem: A 68-year-old man has bothersome moderate-to-severe lower urinary tract symptoms unresponsive to conservative measures; his prostate volume is 45 g, PSA 2.1 ng/ml, and he is considered at high risk of progression. According to NICE CG97, which drug treatment should be offered?

options.A: An alpha-blocker alone, as it is the only option for men with LUTS
options.B: An anticholinergic as first-line therapy for voiding symptoms
options.C: A 5-alpha reductase inhibitor, because the prostate is larger than 30 g and PSA is greater than 1.4 ng/ml with high risk of progression
options.D: A beta-3-adrenoceptor agonist as first-line treatment for these voiding symptoms
options.E: No drug treatment until an episode of acute urinary retention occurs

questions.explanation: CG97 recommendation 1.4.6 is to offer a 5-alpha reductase inhibitor to men with LUTS and a prostate estimated to be larger than 30 g or a PSA level greater than 1.4 ng/ml who are considered at high risk of progression (for example, older men). Recommendation 1.4.7 advises considering a combination of an alpha-blocker and a 5-alpha reductase inhibitor for bothersome moderate to severe LUTS with the same prostate size or PSA thresholds, and drug treatment follows failed or inappropriate conservative management (1.4.1).

references.title: Lower urinary tract symptoms in men: management - Recommendations

questions.topic: Localized renal cell carcinoma - partial nephrectomy
questions.stem: A 55-year-old man is found to have a 3.2 cm (cT1a) contrast-enhancing renal mass, with a normal contralateral kidney and good performance status; surgery is planned with curative intent. According to the EAU renal cell carcinoma guidelines, what is recommended?

options.A: Radical nephrectomy is preferred for all T1 tumours
options.B: Partial nephrectomy should be offered only if the tumour exceeds 7 cm
options.C: Active surveillance should be chosen irrespective of tumour size
options.D: Offer partial nephrectomy to patients with T1 tumours
options.E: Ipsilateral adrenalectomy should be performed routinely at nephrectomy

questions.explanation: The EAU renal cell carcinoma guidelines recommend offering surgery to achieve cure in localised RCC (strong), and specifically to offer partial nephrectomy to patients with T1 tumours (strong). Partial nephrectomy is offered to patients with T2 tumours and a solitary kidney or chronic kidney disease only if technically feasible (weak). Ipsilateral adrenalectomy should not be performed when there is no clinical evidence of adrenal invasion.

references.title: EAU Guidelines on Renal Cell Carcinoma

questions.stem: A 28-year-old man has CT-confirmed uncomplicated acute appendicitis without an appendicolith; he is haemodynamically normal and wishes to avoid surgery. According to the WSES 2020 guidelines, what should the surgical team discuss?

options.A: Non-operative management may only be discussed when an appendicolith is present
options.B: Discuss non-operative management with antibiotics as a safe alternative to surgery in selected patients with uncomplicated acute appendicitis and absence of an appendicolith, advising of the possibility of failure and of misdiagnosing complicated appendicitis
options.C: Non-operative management is contraindicated in all adults
options.D: Antibiotics alone are recommended for complicated appendicitis with an appendicolith
options.E: Non-operative management must not be offered once symptoms have lasted more than 24 hours

questions.explanation: WSES recommendation 2.1.1 (quality of evidence High; strength of recommendation Strong; 1A) states that we recommend discussing non-operative management with antibiotics as a safe alternative to surgery in selected patients with uncomplicated acute appendicitis and absence of appendicolith, advising of the possibility of failure and misdiagnosing complicated appendicitis. The guideline notes that meta-analyses of randomised trials show non-operative management with antibiotics achieves a significantly lower overall complication rate at 5 years and shorter sick leave compared with surgery.

references.title: Diagnosis and treatment of acute appendicitis: 2020 update of the WSES Jerusalem guidelines

questions.stem: A 45-year-old man is listed for elective repair of a primary unilateral inguinal hernia. Which statement matches the international groin hernia guidelines?

options.A: A mesh-based repair technique is recommended for the majority of patients undergoing inguinal hernia repair
options.B: Non-mesh tissue repair should be the first choice for every patient
options.C: Mesh repair increases the risk of recurrence without reducing chronic pain
options.D: Shouldice repair is recommended over mesh repair for all fit adults
options.E: Repair should be postponed until the hernia becomes incarcerated

questions.explanation: The 2023 update of the HerniaSurge international guidelines retained a strong recommendation that a mesh-based repair technique is recommended for the majority of patients undergoing inguinal hernia repair, and states that mesh-based repair reduces the risk of recurrence without increasing the risk for chronic pain. Non-mesh tissue repair is reserved for carefully selected patients after shared decision-making, so it is not the first choice for every patient (B), and repair should not be postponed until incarceration (E).

references.title: International Guidelines for Groin Hernia Management (HerniaSurge) - summary
Update of the international HerniaSurge guidelines for groin hernia management

questions.stem: A 52-year-old woman has Grade II (moderate) acute cholecystitis. Her Charlson Comorbidity Index is 4 and ASA-PS is 2, she is fit for surgery, and she is treated in a centre with experienced laparoscopic surgeons. According to TG18, what is the preferred management?

options.A: Percutaneous cholecystostomy as the first-line treatment
options.B: Delayed cholecystectomy after 8 weeks of antibiotics only
options.C: Immediate open cholecystectomy regardless of severity grading
options.D: Antibiotics alone until organ failure develops
options.E: Early laparoscopic cholecystectomy performed by experienced surgeons, because CCI is 5 or below and ASA-PS is 2 or below

questions.explanation: TG18 recommends early laparoscopic cholecystectomy for Grade II acute cholecystitis when the patient meets the criteria of Charlson Comorbidity Index 5 or below and ASA physical status 2 or below, performed by experienced surgeons; if these criteria are not met, medical treatment and/or gallbladder drainage are given first, with laparoscopic cholecystectomy indicated afterwards. For Grade I disease, early laparoscopic cholecystectomy is the first-line treatment.

references.title: Tokyo Guidelines 2018 flowchart for the management of acute cholecystitis

questions.topic: Surgical site infection - antibiotic prophylaxis indications
questions.stem: According to NICE NG125, antibiotic prophylaxis should be given before all of the following EXCEPT:

options.A: Clean surgery involving the placement of a prosthesis or implant
options.B: Clean-contaminated surgery
options.C: Contaminated surgery
options.D: Clean non-prosthetic uncomplicated surgery

questions.explanation: NG125 recommendation 1.2.12 states that antibiotic prophylaxis should be given before clean surgery involving the placement of a prosthesis or implant, before clean-contaminated surgery, and before contaminated surgery. Recommendation 1.2.13 states that antibiotic prophylaxis should not be used routinely for clean non-prosthetic uncomplicated surgery, which is therefore the exception. Where prophylaxis is used, a single dose given intravenously when anaesthesia is started is advised (1.2.15).

references.title: Surgical site infections: prevention and treatment - Recommendations

questions.stem: A 40-year-old woman with hereditary spherocytosis is listed for elective splenectomy in 10 days' time. According to the UK immunisation guidance (Green Book, chapter 25), what should be done?

options.A: Postpone surgery and give the vaccines 4 to 6 weeks before splenectomy
options.B: Do not vaccinate before surgery; give the first dose on the day of discharge
options.C: Withhold pneumococcal vaccination because splenectomy removes the indication
options.D: Give the vaccines now, up to two weeks before surgery; splenectomy should never be delayed for vaccination

questions.explanation: The Green Book states that vaccines should ideally be given 4 to 6 weeks before elective splenectomy, and where this is not possible, up to two weeks before treatment; this patient's surgery is in 10 days, so vaccination should be given now. If vaccination beforehand is not practicable, splenectomy should never be delayed, and immunisation should then be delayed until at least two weeks after the operation because functional antibody responses may be better from that time. People with asplenia are re-immunised with PPV23 or PCV20 every five years.

references.title: The green book: pneumococcal - Chapter 25 (updated 29 July 2026)

questions.stem: A 68-year-old man is brought to the emergency department 3 hours after the abrupt onset of right-sided weakness and dysphasia. Non-contrast CT shows no intracranial haemorrhage and there are no contraindications to thrombolysis. Which of the following is the most appropriate additional acute treatment?

options.A: Intravenous thrombolysis with alteplase or tenecteplase within 4.5 hours of symptom onset, after excluding intracranial haemorrhage, in a well-organised stroke service
options.B: Intravenous thrombolysis only after waiting 24 hours to confirm the diagnosis with a repeat CT scan
options.C: Withhold all reperfusion treatment and give aspirin 300 mg immediately, since thrombolysis is only licensed for use within 2 hours of onset
options.D: Intravenous heparin infusion to prevent propagation of the infarct before any reperfusion decision is made
options.E: Referral for mechanical thrombectomy only, because thrombolysis is contraindicated whenever a large vessel occlusion is present

questions.explanation: NICE NG128 directs clinicians to technology appraisal guidance on tenecteplase (TA990) and alteplase (TA264) for treating acute ischaemic stroke within 4.5 hours of symptom onset once intracranial haemorrhage has been excluded, and thrombolytics must be given only within a well-organised stroke service with trained staff and neuroradiological support. Aspirin 300 mg is still given within 24 hours once imaging excludes haemorrhage, but it does not replace thrombolysis in a eligible patient. Thrombectomy is offered separately, within 6 hours, alongside thrombolysis when indicated.

references.title: Stroke and transient ischaemic attack in over 16s: diagnosis and initial management - recommendations

questions.stem: A 62-year-old woman develops a dense left hemiparesis and gaze deviation. CT angiography confirms a right internal carotid artery occlusion. She was last known to be well 5 hours ago, baseline imaging shows a small established infarct with salvageable tissue, and there are no contraindications. Which of the following is the most appropriate management?

options.A: Defer all intervention and repeat the imaging in 24 hours before deciding on treatment
options.B: Offer thrombectomy as soon as possible and within 6 hours of symptom onset, together with intravenous thrombolysis if not contraindicated and within the licensed window
options.C: Withhold thrombectomy because intravenous thrombolysis alone is superior beyond 4.5 hours
options.D: Start dual antiplatelet therapy and arrange carotid endarterectomy within 48 hours as the definitive treatment
options.E: Offer thrombectomy only if the occlusion involves the posterior circulation

questions.explanation: NICE NG128 recommends offering thrombectomy as soon as possible and within 6 hours of symptom onset together with intravenous thrombolysis when that is not contraindicated and is within its licensed window. For patients last known well up to 24 hours previously, including wake-up strokes, thrombectomy should be considered when imaging shows salvageable tissue, and it may be considered up to 24 hours in posterior circulation occlusion. Recanalisation therapies must still be delivered within an acute stroke service.

references.title: Stroke and transient ischaemic attack in over 16s: diagnosis and initial management - recommendations

questions.topic: Intracerebral haemorrhage - acute blood pressure management
questions.stem: A 70-year-old hypertensive man presents 3 hours after the acute onset of headache, vomiting and left hemiparesis. The non-contrast CT head is shown. His systolic blood pressure is 175 mm Hg and there are no exclusions to blood pressure lowering. According to NICE guidance, what is the target of rapid blood pressure lowering?

image.alt: CT scan of the brain showing an intracerebral haemorrhage
image.caption: Non-contrast CT head demonstrating a spontaneous intracerebral haemorrhage
image.source: Wikimedia Commons - File:Intracerebral.jpg (CC BY-SA 3.0, Lucien Monfils)

options.A: Lower systolic blood pressure to below 110 mm Hg within 1 hour to minimise haematoma expansion
options.B: Maintain systolic blood pressure between 150 and 220 mm Hg and avoid any reduction during the first 24 hours
options.C: Aim for a systolic blood pressure of 140 mm Hg or lower, ensuring the magnitude of the fall does not exceed 60 mm Hg within 1 hour of starting treatment
options.D: No pharmacological blood pressure lowering is indicated because the haemorrhage is more than 2 hours old
options.E: Reduce systolic blood pressure to 185 mm Hg or lower, which is the threshold for thrombolysis in ischaemic stroke

questions.explanation: NICE NG128 advises considering rapid blood pressure lowering in acute intracerebral haemorrhage when systolic pressure is between 150 and 220 mm Hg and there are no exclusions, with the aim of reaching a systolic pressure of 140 mm Hg or lower while ensuring the total fall does not exceed 60 mm Hg within 1 hour of starting treatment. Excessively rapid or deep lowering risks cerebral hypoperfusion. The 185/110 mm Hg threshold applies to thrombolysis candidacy in acute ischaemic stroke, not to intracerebral haemorrhage.

references.title: Stroke and transient ischaemic attack in over 16s: diagnosis and initial management - recommendations

questions.stem: A 34-year-old man with known epilepsy is still convulsing 7 minutes after the start of a generalised tonic-clonic seizure in the emergency department. Intravenous access is established. Which of the following best describes the recommended treatment sequence?

options.A: Give a second-line intravenous antiepileptic immediately as first-line treatment, because the seizure has passed 5 minutes
options.B: Begin continuous general anaesthesia as first-line therapy while awaiting EEG confirmation
options.C: Treat with intramuscular antibiotics first, since sepsis is the most common cause of prolonged seizures in adults
options.D: Give a benzodiazepine first; if the seizure has not stopped after 5 to 10 minutes give a second benzodiazepine dose, then treat with intravenous levetiracetam, phenytoin or valproate
options.E: Administer a loading dose of phenytoin first and reserve benzodiazepines for patients who are not in status epilepticus

questions.explanation: NICE NG217 defines convulsive status epilepticus as a continuous convulsive seizure lasting 5 minutes or longer, or two or more seizures without full recovery of consciousness. First-line treatment is a benzodiazepine (intravenous lorazepam in hospital, or buccal midazolam or rectal diazepam in the community), with a second benzodiazepine dose if the seizure has not terminated after 5 to 10 minutes. Second-line treatment is intravenous levetiracetam, phenytoin or valproate, with valproate used only in line with MHRA advice on its precautions.

references.title: Epilepsies in children, young people and adults - treating status epilepticus, repeated or cluster seizures, and prolonged seizures

questions.stem: A 58-year-old man had 20 minutes of expressive dysphasia and right arm clumsiness which resolved completely. He is now neurologically normal. His ABCD2 score is 2. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step?

options.A: Arrange a routine outpatient clinic appointment in 2 weeks with an ABCD2-guided priority
options.B: Discharge with clopidogrel 75 mg daily only and no specialist assessment, because his ABCD2 score is low
options.C: Admit for 48 hours of observation before starting any antiplatelet medication
options.D: Start low-dose aspirin 75 mg daily and review in 1 month if symptoms recur
options.E: Give aspirin 300 mg immediately and arrange for him to be assessed by a specialist service within 24 hours

questions.explanation: NICE NG128 recommends offering aspirin 300 mg immediately to people with suspected transient ischaemic attack, in addition to starting clopidogrel once the diagnosis is confirmed, and referring for specialist assessment within 24 hours of presentation. Guidance explicitly states that the ABCD2 score should not be used to assess the risk of a subsequent stroke or to determine the urgency of referral. Delaying antiplatelet loading or relying on a low ABCD2 score risks early recurrent stroke.

references.title: Stroke and transient ischaemic attack in over 16s: diagnosis and initial management - recommendations

questions.stem: A 24-year-old woman presents with daily morning headaches, transient visual obscurations and a pulsatile sensation in her ears. Fundoscopy of her right eye is shown. Which of the following best describes the finding and its significance?

image.alt: Fundus photograph of the right eye showing severe papilloedema with blurred optic disc margins
image.caption: Fundal photograph showing severe papilloedema in the right eye
image.source: Wikimedia Commons - File:Fundal photograph showing severe papilloedema in the right eye.jpg (CC BY 2.0, Bansal, Dabbs and Long)

options.A: A normal optic disc with sharp margins; the symptoms are diagnostic of migraine with aura
options.B: Blurred, elevated optic disc margins with vessel blurring consistent with papilloedema, indicating raised intracranial pressure that requires urgent intracranial pressure work-up
options.C: Pale optic disc with lost cupping, indicating established optic atrophy from prior glaucoma
options.D: Hard exudates in a macular star pattern, indicating hypertensive retinopathy
options.E: A dark red retinal spot with a white surround, indicating central retinal artery occlusion

questions.explanation: The photograph shows severe papilloedema, that is, swelling of the optic disc caused by increased intracranial pressure, which fits her headache pattern, morning worsening and transient visual obscurations. Papilloedema is an abnormal finding that mandates urgent assessment of intracranial pressure with neuroimaging and, when appropriate, lumbar puncture after imaging. The other options describe normal ageing, optic atrophy, diabetic or hypertensive retinopathy, and retinal artery occlusion, none of which produce disc swelling.

references.title: Fundal photograph showing severe papilloedema in the right eye

questions.topic: Parkinson's disease - motor and non-motor complications
questions.stem: A 66-year-old man with Parkinson's disease of 8 years' duration, treated with levodopa, reports increasingly vivid visual hallucinations of unfamiliar people in the house, with distress to his family. Which of the following is the most appropriate pharmacological step?

options.A: Increase levodopa dose, because hallucinations always indicate dopaminergic under-treatment
options.B: Stop levodopa abruptly and switch to a dopamine agonist to reduce hallucination risk
