options.C: Offer a drug holiday by stopping all antiparkinsonian medication for a week
options.D: Start olanzapine 5 mg daily as the preferred atypical antipsychotic in Parkinson's disease
options.E: Offer quetiapine, and if that is ineffective consider clozapine; do not offer olanzapine

questions.explanation: NICE NG71 recommends offering quetiapine for hallucinations in Parkinson's disease and, if quetiapine is ineffective, considering clozapine with haematological monitoring, while olanzapine should not be offered because it worsens parkinsonism. Levodopa remains first-line therapy when motor symptoms impact quality of life, so stopping it or using drug holidays would worsen disability; NG71 advises against drug holidays. Hallucinations in established Parkinson's disease are typically a complication of therapy or disease progression rather than under-treatment.

references.title: Parkinson's disease in adults - recommendations

questions.stem: A 74-year-old woman has a 2-year history of progressive amnesia and disorientation with a Montreal Cognitive Assessment score of 18, consistent with mild to moderate Alzheimer's disease. She lives at home with support. Which of the following is the most appropriate pharmacological treatment?

options.A: Memantine as first-line monotherapy for all stages of Alzheimer's disease
options.B: Routine low-dose risperidone to prevent agitation and wandering
options.C: A cholinesterase inhibitor such as donepezil, galantamine or rivastigmine
options.D: High-dose vitamin E and ginseng supplements as disease-modifying therapy
options.E: No pharmacological treatment until the patient can no longer dress herself

questions.explanation: NICE NG97 recommends offering a cholinesterase inhibitor (donepezil, galantamine or rivastigmine) for mild to moderate Alzheimer's disease. Memantine is reserved for moderate disease when cholinesterase inhibitors are contraindicated or not tolerated, or for severe Alzheimer's disease, and may be added to a cholinesterase inhibitor in severe disease. Antipsychotics should only be considered when there is a risk of harm to the person or others, or severe distress from agitation, hallucinations or delusions, and ginseng and vitamin E are not recommended.

references.title: Dementia: assessment, management and support for people living with dementia and their carers - recommendations

questions.stem: A 22-year-old woman gets disabling migraine attacks twice a week. Simple analgesic taken early gives only partial relief. Which of the following is the recommended acute treatment strategy?

options.A: Combination of an oral ergotamine preparation with a weak opioid
options.B: Combination therapy with an oral triptan plus an NSAID, or an oral triptan plus paracetamol
options.C: Propranolol 40 mg twice daily started as sole acute therapy for every attack
options.D: Immediate intravenous metoclopramide monotherapy for every attack in the emergency department

questions.explanation: For the acute treatment of migraine, NICE CG150 recommends offering combination therapy with an oral triptan and an NSAID, or an oral triptan and paracetamol, taking account of preference, comorbidities and adverse events. If the person prefers a single agent, monotherapy with an oral triptan, NSAID, aspirin 900 mg or paracetamol may be considered. Ergots and opioids should not be offered, and prophylaxis such as propranolol is used to prevent attacks rather than treat them.

references.title: Headaches in over 12s: diagnosis and management - recommendations

questions.stem: A 32-year-old woman with relapsing-remitting multiple sclerosis develops new left leg weakness 5 days ago, lasting more than 24 hours after 18 months of stability. Urinalysis is negative and she has no fever. The weakness prevents her from walking to work. Which of the following is the recommended treatment for this relapse?

options.A: Observe for 3 months because symptoms present for less than 3 months cannot be diagnosed as a relapse
options.B: Start or escalate a disease-modifying therapy and give no acute treatment
options.C: Intravenous immunoglobulin 0.4 g/kg daily for 5 days as first-line therapy
options.D: Oral methylprednisolone 0.5 g once daily for 5 days
options.E: Plasma exchange within 24 hours because more than 72 hours have elapsed since symptom onset

questions.explanation: NICE NG220 defines a relapse as new or worsened symptoms lasting more than 24 hours after a stable period of at least 1 month in the absence of infection, and recommends offering treatment for relapses that affect usual activities as early as possible and within 14 days of onset. The recommended treatment is oral methylprednisolone 0.5 g daily for 5 days, and non-specialists should discuss whether steroids are needed because not every relapse requires treatment. Infection must be excluded first, and symptoms lasting more than 3 months should not routinely be diagnosed as a relapse.

references.title: Multiple sclerosis in adults: management - recommendations

questions.topic: Depression - first-line treatment of a less severe episode
questions.stem: A 30-year-old man reports 6 weeks of low mood and anhedonia with a PHQ-9 score of 10 (less severe depression). He has no suicidal ideation and wants to start treatment. Which of the following is the recommended first-line approach?

options.A: Do not routinely offer antidepressant medication as first-line; offer a guided self-help or psychological intervention such as group behavioural activation, matched to his preference
options.B: Start fluoxetine 20 mg daily immediately as first-line treatment for everyone with less severe depression
options.C: Withhold all treatment for 8 weeks to see whether symptoms remit spontaneously
options.D: Refer immediately for electroconvulsive therapy because the episode has lasted more than 1 month
options.E: Offer an antipsychotic augmentation strategy before any psychological intervention

questions.explanation: NICE NG222 states that antidepressant medication should not be routinely offered as first-line treatment for less severe depression, and should only be offered if that is the person's informed preference. First-line options guided by table 1 include guided self-help materials based on CBT or behavioural activation, group behavioural activation and other psychological interventions matched to clinical need and preference. Escalation to medication or combination treatment applies to more severe depression (PHQ-9 of 16 or above).

references.title: Depression in adults: treatment and management - recommendations

questions.stem: A 19-year-old university student is started on sertraline for more severe depression after a full assessment and a shared management plan. When should she be reviewed after starting the medication?

options.A: Within 6 weeks, because antidepressants need a full 6 weeks to work and early review is unnecessary
options.B: Within 3 days, because serotonin syndrome typically presents on day 2
options.C: 1 week after starting the antidepressant, because she is aged 18 to 25, and thereafter no later than 4 weeks (the usual first review for others is within 2 weeks)
options.D: Only when she requests an appointment, since side effects are managed by the pharmacy
options.E: At 3 months, aligned with the minimum duration of antidepressant treatment

questions.explanation: When prescribing antidepressants, NICE NG222 says the first review will usually be within 2 weeks to check symptoms and side effects, but should be 1 week after starting if the prescription is for a person aged 18 to 25 years or if there is particular concern about suicide risk, with further review no later than 4 weeks. It also advises telling the person that an effect, if the medicine is going to work, is usually seen within 4 weeks. Treatment typically continues for at least 6 months after remission but must be reviewed regularly.

references.title: Depression in adults: treatment and management - recommendations

questions.stem: A 28-year-old woman diagnosed with bipolar I disorder presents with 5 days of reduced need for sleep, pressured speech, spending sprees and grandiosity. She has been taking fluoxetine 40 mg daily for presumed unipolar depression. Which of the following is the most appropriate management?

options.A: Continue fluoxetine unchanged and add lithium at the next routine appointment
options.B: Start lamotrigine as first-line acute treatment because it is a mood stabiliser with a benign side-effect profile
options.C: Offer fluoxetine plus olanzapine combination, which is first-line for this presentation
options.D: Wait for spontaneous resolution because antidepressant-associated hypomania does not need treatment
options.E: Stop the antidepressant and start an antipsychotic such as haloperidol, olanzapine, quetiapine or risperidone, with close monitoring of mental state and side effects

questions.explanation: NICE CG185 recommends that if a person taking an antidepressant alone develops mania or hypomania, the antidepressant should be stopped and treatment started with an antipsychotic - haloperidol, olanzapine, quetiapine or risperidone - with monitoring of mental state and side effects. Lamotrigine should not be offered as treatment for mania, and the fluoxetine-olanzapine or fluoxetine-quetiapine combinations apply to bipolar depression, not acute mania. Lithium is used for long-term prevention rather than as the acute agent in this scenario.

references.title: Bipolar disorder: assessment and management - recommendations

questions.stem: A 21-year-old man is referred to the early intervention in psychosis service with 3 months of persecutory ideas, social withdrawal and auditory hallucinations. Physical assessment is complete. Which of the following is the recommended package of care at first presentation?

options.A: Offer oral antipsychotic medication together with psychological interventions - individual CBT and family intervention - and a care plan made in collaboration with the person
options.B: Offer antipsychotic medication alone, because psychological interventions are ineffective in a first episode
options.C: Offer individual CBT alone and defer any medication until after 6 months of unsupported follow-up
options.D: Start an antidepressant and review in primary care in 6 weeks
options.E: Begin clozapine immediately as the first-line antipsychotic for all first-episode presentations

questions.explanation: NICE CG178 recommends that people with a first episode psychosis are offered oral antipsychotic medication in conjunction with psychological interventions, specifically family intervention and individual CBT, delivered as described in the guideline, with a care plan written collaboratively after assessment. Early intervention in psychosis services should be accessible to all people with a first episode or first presentation of psychosis irrespective of age or duration of untreated psychosis. Antipsychotic medication should not be started for a first presentation in primary care unless in consultation with a consultant psychiatrist.

references.title: Psychosis and schizophrenia in adults: prevention and management - recommendations

questions.topic: Attention deficit hyperactivity disorder in adults - medication
questions.stem: A 28-year-old man with confirmed ADHD has taken methylphenidate 60 mg daily for 6 weeks with only partial benefit and troublesome side effects. He wishes to continue medication. What is the recommended next step?

options.A: Add an antipsychotic to augment the stimulant response
options.B: Continue methylphenidate unchanged for a further 6 months before considering any change
options.C: Stop medication and offer only behavioural strategies because adult ADHD does not respond to drugs
options.D: Switch to lisdexamfetamine; if that trial is inadequate or the drug is not tolerated, consider atomoxetine as an alternative
options.E: Switch directly to an antipsychotic because motor side effects indicate a different diagnosis

questions.explanation: For adults, NICE NG87 recommends lisdexamfetamine or methylphenidate as first-line pharmacological treatment; if there is no response to an adequate trial of the first drug, an alternative should be tried, and a stimulant is only switched after a 6-week trial at an adequate dose. If both stimulants are ineffective or not tolerated, atomoxetine may be offered, with specialist review before stopping all medication. In children and young people aged 5 and over, methylphenidate is first-line, with lisdexamfetamine considered after a 6-week methylphenidate trial.

references.title: Attention deficit hyperactivity disorder: diagnosis and management - recommendations

questions.stem: A 52-year-old alcohol-dependent man is admitted for medically assisted withdrawal. On day 3 he becomes confused, frightened and visually hallucinated with tremor, tachycardia and hypertension. Which of the following is the recommended first-line treatment?

options.A: Haloperidol alone as monotherapy, with no benzodiazepine
options.B: Oral lorazepam as first-line treatment; if symptoms persist or oral medication is declined, offer parenteral lorazepam or haloperidol
options.C: Intravenous haloperidol first, reserving lorazepam for seizures
options.D: No pharmacological treatment; symptoms resolve with reassurance alone
options.E: High-dose antipsychotic depot injection followed by discharge

questions.explanation: NICE CG100 recommends oral lorazepam as first-line treatment for delirium tremens, offering parenteral lorazepam or haloperidol if symptoms persist or oral medication is declined, and reviewing the withdrawal drug regimen if delirium tremens develops during treatment. For the withdrawal syndrome itself, a benzodiazepine or carbamazepine is offered, with a symptom-triggered regimen used in hospital or settings with 24-hour monitoring. Clomethiazole is an alternative restricted to inpatient use with caution.

references.title: Alcohol-use disorders: diagnosis and management of physical complications - recommendations

questions.topic: Glaucoma - initial treatment of chronic open angle glaucoma
questions.stem: A 58-year-old man is newly diagnosed with non-advanced chronic open angle glaucoma: Goldmann applanation tonometry shows intraocular pressure of 26 mm Hg, with reproducible visual field loss and optic nerve head damage. He has no pigment dispersion syndrome. Which of the following is the recommended initial treatment?

options.A: No treatment until intraocular pressure exceeds 30 mm Hg
options.B: Immediate trabeculectomy as first-line surgery for all newly diagnosed cases
options.C: Timolol 0.5% eye drops twice daily as the mandatory first step in every patient
options.D: Refer for cataract surgery, since raised intraocular pressure is usually lens related
options.E: Offer 360-degree selective laser trabeculoplasty (SLT), which can delay the need for eye drops and may be repeated if its effect reduces

questions.explanation: NICE NG81 recommends offering 360-degree selective laser trabeculoplasty to people with newly diagnosed chronic open angle glaucoma that is not advanced (excluding pigment dispersion syndrome), and a second SLT may be considered if the initial effect diminishes. People are told that SLT can delay the need for eye drops but does not remove the chance they will be needed. Prostaglandin analogues are offered when people decline or are unsuitable for SLT, or need additional treatment, rather than being the automatic first step.

references.title: Glaucoma: diagnosis and management - recommendations

questions.stem: A 72-year-old woman reports sudden distortion of central vision in the right eye (metamorphopsia) over 10 days. Fundoscopy suggests active late (wet) age-related macular degeneration. Which of the following is the recommended referral and treatment pathway?

options.A: Routine referral with a target of assessment within 6 weeks, since painless visual loss can wait
options.B: Refer to a macula service within 1 working day and start high-dose antioxidant vitamins while awaiting treatment
options.C: Make an urgent referral to a macula service within 1 working day, and offer intravitreal anti-VEGF treatment as soon as possible, within 14 days of referral
options.D: Observation for 3 months with home monitoring grids before any referral
options.E: Refer for photodynamic therapy, which is the preferred first-line treatment for all wet AMD

questions.explanation: NICE NG82 recommends an urgent referral to a macula service for people with suspected active late (wet) AMD, whether or not they report visual impairment, normally made within 1 working day. For eyes with confirmed wet active AMD for which antiangiogenic treatment is recommended, treatment should be offered as soon as possible, within 14 days of referral to the macular service, and intravitreal anti-VEGF is the recommended pharmacological treatment. Smoking cessation is advised as a modifiable risk factor.

references.title: Age-related macular degeneration - recommendations

questions.stem: A 55-year-old man with type 2 diabetes is found on screening to have proliferative diabetic retinopathy in both eyes with no vitreous haemorrhage. Which of the following is the recommended first treatment?

options.A: Panretinal photocoagulation, which is usually the first treatment for most people and is completed within 4 weeks of starting
options.B: Intravitreal anti-VEGF as first-line treatment for every patient, with laser reserved only for failures
options.C: Immediate vitrectomy in both eyes before any laser is considered
options.D: Observation with 6-monthly review until tractional retinal detachment develops

questions.explanation: NICE NG242 states that panretinal photocoagulation is usually the first treatment for most people with proliferative diabetic retinopathy and should be offered when the person is first diagnosed, with the course completed within 4 weeks of starting treatment; for high-risk characteristics or difficulty attending, treatment can be started the same day. Anti-VEGF is offered for activity persisting after complete panretinal photocoagulation, and vitrectomy is considered for non-clearing vitreous haemorrhage lasting 3 months or for macula-involving retinal detachment.

references.title: Diabetic retinopathy: management and monitoring - recommendations

questions.stem: A 72-year-old woman describes a 3-week history of new temporal headache, jaw claudication while chewing and tenderness of the scalp. Her erythrocyte sedimentation rate is 4 mm/h. Which of the following is the correct interpretation?

options.A: A normal ESR excludes giant cell arteritis, so no further action is needed
options.B: Giant cell arteritis is only diagnosable if the C-reactive protein is also raised
options.C: Symptoms are typical of tension-type headache and should be reviewed in 3 months
options.D: Temporal artery biopsy is unnecessary because jaw claudication has 100% specificity
options.E: A normal ESR does not exclude giant cell arteritis - consider blood tests and follow local pathways for suspected giant cell (temporal) arteritis

questions.explanation: For adults with scalp tenderness or jaw claudication suggestive of temporal arteritis, NICE NG127 advises considering blood tests and following local pathways for suspected giant cell (temporal) arteritis, and explicitly warns that a normal ESR does not exclude the diagnosis. This matters because untreated arteritis carries a high risk of permanent visual loss from anterior ischaemic optic neuropathy. Diagnosis therefore rests on the clinical picture together with pathway-based investigation, not on a single normal inflammatory marker.

references.title: Suspected neurological conditions: recognition and referral - recommendations for adults aged over 16

questions.stem: An 80-year-old woman has a unilateral cataract. Best-corrected visual acuity in the affected eye is 6/12, but she reports glare when driving at night and has stopped reading. She wants surgery. Which of the following best reflects NICE guidance on referral?

options.A: Surgery must be deferred until visual acuity falls below 6/24 in the affected eye
options.B: Surgery should be offered only if both eyes are affected simultaneously
options.C: The decision is based on a discussion of how the cataract affects vision and quality of life and whether the person wants surgery - access should not be restricted on the basis of visual acuity
options.D: Referral is inappropriate because one eye still has normal acuity
options.E: Referral should wait until the cataract is 'mature' and blocks all red reflex

questions.explanation: NICE NG77 says the decision to refer a person with a cataract for surgery should be based on a discussion covering how the cataract affects vision and quality of life, whether one or both eyes are affected, what surgery involves including risks and benefits, how quality of life might be affected without surgery, and whether the person wants surgery. It explicitly states not to restrict access to cataract surgery on the basis of visual acuity. Patient-reported functional limitation such as glare and reading difficulty therefore drives referral, not a fixed acuity cut-off.

references.title: Cataracts in adults: management - recommendations

questions.stem: A 3-year-old child has had 2 days of fever and right ear pain. Otoscopy is shown. She is systemically well, there is no otorrhoea and neither ear is discharging, and she has no history of immunosuppression or craniofacial abnormality. Which of the following is the most appropriate management?

image.alt: Otoscopic image of acute otitis media showing mucopurulent exudate behind a bulging tympanic membrane
image.caption: Otoscopic appearance of acute otitis media with bulging tympanic membrane and mucopurulent exudate
image.source: Wikimedia Commons - File:Acute Otitis Media Stage of Resolution.jpg (CC BY 4.0, Michael Hawke MD)

options.A: No immediate antibiotic; give a back-up antibiotic prescription to be used if symptoms do not start to improve within 3 days or worsen rapidly or significantly
options.B: Immediate amoxicillin for every child with acute otitis media and fever
options.C: Immediate referral for grommet insertion before any medical treatment
options.D: Immediate intravenous co-amoxiclav and admission, since middle ear infection always requires parenteral therapy

questions.explanation: NICE NG91 recommends considering no antibiotic prescription or a back-up antibiotic prescription for most children with acute otitis media, advising that the back-up prescription is used if symptoms do not start to improve within 3 days or worsen rapidly or significantly at any time. Immediate antibiotics are reserved for those more likely to benefit, such as any child with otorrhoea or those under 2 years with infection in both ears, as well as those who are systemically very unwell or at high risk of complications. When an antibiotic is needed, first-choice oral treatment is amoxicillin for 5 to 7 days.

references.title: Otitis media (acute): antimicrobial prescribing - recommendations

questions.stem: A 25-year-old woman has nasal congestion and facial pain for 5 days without improvement but is systemically well, has no high-risk comorbidity and no signs of a more serious illness. Which of the following is the recommended management?

options.A: Immediate intravenous antibiotics and CT sinuses the same day
options.B: Immediate oral co-amoxiclav for 10 days for every adult with acute sinusitis
options.C: Immediate phenoxymethylpenicillin for all patients regardless of severity
options.D: Immediate referral for endoscopic sinus surgery because symptoms have lasted 5 days
options.E: Consider no antibiotic prescription or a back-up antibiotic prescription with self-care advice, reserving immediate antibiotics for people who are systemically very unwell or at high risk of complications

questions.explanation: NICE NG79 recommends considering no antibiotic prescription or a back-up antibiotic prescription for acute sinusitis in people who are not systemically very unwell and not at high risk of complications, because most improve without antibiotics. Immediate antibiotic treatment is offered to people who are systemically very unwell, have symptoms and signs of a more serious illness or condition, or are at high risk of complications. Where an antibiotic is indicated, first choice is phenoxymethylpenicillin 500 mg four times a day for 5 days, with co-amoxiclav reserved for those who are systemically very unwell or at high risk.

references.title: Sinusitis (acute): antimicrobial prescribing - recommendations

questions.stem: A 55-year-old woman reports brief episodes of spinning provoked by rolling over in bed. The Dix-Hallpike manoeuvre reproduces the vertigo with a characteristic latency and fatiguing nystagmus. Cervical spine is stable. Which of the following is the recommended treatment?

options.A: Betahistine four times daily as first-line treatment
options.B: A canalith repositioning manoeuvre such as the Epley manoeuvre
options.C: Urgent MRI brain before any physical treatment is attempted
options.D: Prolonged bed rest with sedatives for 6 weeks

questions.explanation: NICE NG127 recommends offering the Hallpike manoeuvre to check for benign paroxysmal positional vertigo when a clinician trained in its use is available, and, if BPPV is diagnosed, offering a canalith repositioning manoeuvre such as the Epley manoeuvre if the person does not have unstable cervical spine disease. If no trained clinician is available, the person should be referred in accordance with local pathways. BPPV is also common after head injury or labyrinthitis.

references.title: Suspected neurological conditions: recognition and referral - recommendations for adults aged over 16

questions.topic: Suspected head and neck cancer referral
questions.stem: A 58-year-old man has had persistent unexplained hoarseness for 6 weeks with no recent upper respiratory infection and no response to simple measures. He has no palatal or vocal fold lesion on basic examination. Which of the following is the recommended action?

options.A: Wait a further 3 months for spontaneous resolution before any referral
options.B: Treat with 3 months of proton pump inhibitor therapy and review
options.C: Consider a suspected cancer pathway referral for laryngeal cancer, because persistent unexplained hoarseness in a person aged 45 or over warrants urgent assessment
options.D: Arrange a routine speech and language therapy appointment without medical review

questions.explanation: NICE NG12 recommends considering a suspected cancer pathway referral for laryngeal cancer in people aged 45 and over with persistent and unexplained hoarseness, or an unexplained lump in the neck. For oral cancer, consider a suspected cancer pathway referral for unexplained oral ulceration lasting more than 3 weeks or a persistent unexplained lump in the neck, and urgent dental assessment for an unexplained oral lump or erythroplakia or erythroleukoplakia. Delaying referral risks progression before treatment.

references.title: Suspected cancer: recognition and referral - recommendations organised by site of cancer

questions.stem: A 20-year-old university student has a 2-day sore throat and mild fever. She is systemically well, has no comorbidity and is not at high risk of complications; her FeverPAIN score is 2. Which of the following is the most appropriate prescribing decision?

options.A: Immediate phenoxymethylpenicillin 500 mg four times a day for every low FeverPAIN score
options.B: Immediate amoxicillin because most sore throats are streptococcal
options.C: Immediate clarithromycin as first-line treatment for all patients
options.D: No immediate antibiotic - offer a back-up prescription to be used if symptoms do not improve within 3 to 5 days, with first-choice treatment being phenoxymethylpenicillin 500 mg four times a day (or 1,000 mg twice a day) for 5 to 10 days

questions.explanation: For acute sore throat, NICE NG84 recommends considering either no antibiotic prescription with advice or a back-up antibiotic prescription when complications are unlikely, with the back-up prescription used if symptoms do not start to improve within 3 to 5 days or worsen rapidly or significantly. Immediate treatment is reserved for those with a FeverPAIN score of 4 or 5 or Centor score of 3 or 4 after considering harms and benefits, and for people who are systemically very unwell or at high risk of complications. The first-choice oral antibiotic is phenoxymethylpenicillin, with clarithromycin as an alternative in penicillin allergy for people who are not pregnant.

references.title: Sore throat (acute): antimicrobial prescribing - recommendations

questions.stem: A 19-year-old woman with type 1 diabetes presents with vomiting, abdominal pain, Kussmaul breathing, glucose 24 mmol/L, venous pH 7.12 and ketonaemia. After initial 0.9% sodium chloride resuscitation she is started on a fixed-rate intravenous insulin infusion. Which insulin infusion rate is recommended as the starting dose in adults with diabetic ketoacidosis?

options.A: 0.05 units/kg/h, which is the standard starting rate for all adults with DKA
options.B: 0.075 units/kg/h, titrated upward only if the ketone level does not fall
options.C: 0.1 units/kg/h, with an optional 0.1 units/kg bolus if obtaining venous access is delayed
options.D: 0.2 units/kg/h, doubled from the historical dose to shorten time to resolution

questions.explanation: The 2024 consensus report on hyperglycemic crises recommends a fixed-rate intravenous insulin infusion started at 0.1 units/kg/h, with an initial bolus of 0.1 units/kg only if obtaining venous access will be delayed. Once blood glucose falls below 250 mg/dL (13.9 mmol/L), 5-10% dextrose is added to the 0.9% saline and the infusion is reduced to 0.05 units/kg/h. Isotonic saline is the recommended initial resuscitation fluid in most guidelines.

references.title: Hyperglycemic Crises in Adults With Diabetes: A Consensus Report
6. Glycemic Goals, Hypoglycemia, and Hyperglycemic Crises: Standards of Care in Diabetes-2026

questions.stem: A 68-year-old man with type 2 diabetes has UACR 300 mg/g, eGFR 45 mL/min/1.73 m2, and blood pressure controlled on maximally tolerated lisinopril. He is also on metformin and semaglutide. According to the ADA Standards of Care in Diabetes-2026, which additional strategy can be considered to reduce kidney and cardiovascular risk?

options.A: Add a GLP-1 receptor agonist alone, because albuminuria only falls when glucose lowering is intensified
options.B: Simultaneously initiate an SGLT2 inhibitor and the nonsteroidal MRA finerenone, because his UACR is at least 100 mg/g with eGFR 30-90 on a renin-angiotensin system inhibitor
options.C: Stop lisinopril and switch to an angiotensin receptor blocker plus a direct renin inhibitor for dual blockade
options.D: Add the steroidal mineralocorticoid receptor antagonist spironolactone on top of lisinopril as first choice
options.E: Defer kidney-directed therapy and intensify only diuretic treatment until eGFR falls below 30

questions.explanation: ADA 2026 Recommendation 11.9 states that simultaneous initiation of an SGLT2 inhibitor and finerenone can be considered in adults with type 2 diabetes and UACR of at least 100 mg/g with eGFR 30-90 who are on a renin-angiotensin system inhibitor, based on evidence of safety and beneficial effects on albuminuria. Both SGLT2 inhibitors and finerenone mediate most of their benefit through reduction of albuminuria, and RAS blockade should already be at maximally tolerated dose. Dual renin-angiotensin system blockade is not recommended.

references.title: 11. Chronic Kidney Disease and Risk Management: Standards of Care in Diabetes-2026

questions.stem: A 46-year-old woman is found to have a dominant predominantly cystic thyroid nodule that is difficult to palpate. Which of the following statements about fine-needle aspiration of thyroid nodules is correct?

options.A: Palpation-guided FNA is preferred in all cases because it avoids radiation exposure from ultrasound
options.B: FNA should be deferred until scintigraphy confirms a cold nodule, since hot nodules never require sampling
options.C: Cytology results should be reported as simply benign or malignant without any structured classification system
options.D: Ultrasound-guided FNA is preferred when the likelihood of a nondiagnostic sample is high, for example nodules with more than 25%-50% cystic component or nodules that are difficult to palpate
options.E: FNA is contraindicated in nodules that are posteriorly located within the thyroid lobe

questions.explanation: The ATA 2015 guideline states that FNA is the procedure of choice when clinically indicated, and that ultrasound-guided FNA is preferred when there is a higher likelihood of a nondiagnostic result (more than 25%-50% cystic component) or sampling error such as difficult-to-palpate or posterior nodules. It also recommends reporting cytology using the Bethesda System for Reporting Thyroid Cytopathology. Scintigraphy is reserved for low-TSH nodules and does not replace FNA of nonfunctioning nodules that meet size criteria.

references.title: 2015 American Thyroid Association Management Guidelines for Adult Patients with Thyroid Nodules and Differentiated Thyroid Cancer: The American Thyroid Association Guidelines Task Force on Thyroid Nodules and Differentiated Thyroid Cancer

questions.stem: The image shows a thyroid fine-needle aspiration smear from a 39-year-old woman with a 1.8 cm solid hyperechoic nodule. The smear shows papillary structures with true fibrovascular cores, nuclear grooves, pale chromatin and intranuclear cytoplasmic inclusions. Which diagnosis best fits these cytological features?

image.alt: Thyroid FNA smear showing papillary structures with nuclear grooves and intranuclear cytoplasmic inclusions
image.caption: Thyroid fine-needle aspiration showing the nuclear features of papillary thyroid carcinoma
image.source: Wikimedia Commons – File:Papillary Carcinoma of the Thyroid.jpg (Ed Uthman, MD, CC BY-SA 2.0)

options.A: Medullary thyroid carcinoma
options.B: Follicular thyroid carcinoma
options.C: Papillary thyroid carcinoma
options.D: Anaplastic (undifferentiated) thyroid carcinoma
options.E: Primary thyroid lymphoma

questions.explanation: Nuclear grooves, intranuclear cytoplasmic inclusions, pale chromatin, nuclear overlapping and psammoma bodies are the dependable cytomorphological features used to diagnose papillary thyroid carcinoma on cytology. Follicular carcinoma requires demonstration of capsular or vascular invasion on histology, medullary carcinoma arises from parafollicular C cells, and anaplastic carcinoma shows marked pleomorphism rather than these nuclear features.

references.title: Value of Combined Cytomorphological Parameters in Improving Diagnostic Accuracy of Papillary Thyroid Carcinoma on Cytology - The Five Dependable Features

questions.stem: A 42-year-old woman with new-onset hypertension, central obesity, proximal myopathy and violaceous striae is being investigated for Cushing syndrome. Which of the following is recommended as an initial screening test?

options.A: Random serum cortisol measured at any time of day
options.B: Late-night salivary cortisol (two measurements)
options.C: Plasma ACTH concentration
options.D: Insulin tolerance test

questions.explanation: The Endocrine Society guideline recommends one of four high-accuracy initial tests: two urine free cortisol measurements, two late-night salivary cortisol measurements, a 1 mg overnight dexamethasone suppression test, or a longer low-dose dexamethasone suppression test. Random serum cortisol, random plasma ACTH and the insulin tolerance test are recommended against for initial testing. The insulin tolerance test is reserved for assessing the hypothalamic-pituitary-adrenal axis, not for screening.

references.title: Diagnosis of Cushing's Syndrome Guideline Resources

questions.stem: A 58-year-old man with newly diagnosed primary hypothyroidism weighs 70 kg. He is under 65 years of age and has no history of cardiovascular disease. According to NICE guidance, which starting levothyroxine regimen should be considered?

options.A: 1.6 micrograms/kg body weight per day, rounded to the nearest 25 micrograms
options.B: 25-50 micrograms per day with gradual titration, because all adults start low
options.C: Liothyronine alone, because it is more effective than levothyroxine
options.D: Natural thyroid extract in preference to levothyroxine
options.E: A dose titrated to suppress TSH to below the reference range

questions.explanation: NICE NG145 recommends considering levothyroxine at 1.6 micrograms/kg/day rounded to the nearest 25 micrograms for adults under 65 with primary hypothyroidism and no cardiovascular disease history. The lower starting dose of 25-50 micrograms with titration is reserved for adults aged 65 and over and those with cardiovascular disease. Liothyronine is not offered routinely, natural thyroid extract is not recommended, and TSH should be kept within the reference range rather than suppressed.

references.title: Thyroid disease: assessment and management - Recommendations

questions.stem: A 62-year-old man is incidentally found to have asymptomatic primary hyperparathyroidism with serum calcium 0.9 mg/dL (0.22 mmol/L) above the upper limit of normal and eGFR 78 mL/min. Dual-energy X-ray absorptiometry shows a T-score of -2.8 at the femoral neck and vertebral fracture assessment reveals a previously undiagnosed L2 fracture. Which of the following best guides the decision on surgery?

options.A: Surgery is not indicated because the calcium elevation is less than 1.6 mg/dL above the upper limit of normal
options.B: Surgery is only indicated once eGFR falls below 30 mL/min, regardless of skeletal findings
options.C: His vertebral fracture is irrelevant because only fragility fractures of the hip count toward surgical eligibility
options.D: Observation with annual calcium measurement is appropriate until the T-score falls to -3.5
options.E: Parathyroidectomy should be offered, because a T-score of -2.5 or worse at any measured site or a vertebral fracture identified on imaging are both surgical criteria

questions.explanation: The Fourth International Workshop guidelines for asymptomatic primary hyperparathyroidism include skeletal involvement as part of the criteria for surgery: a T-score of -2.5 or below at lumbar spine, total hip, femoral neck or distal one-third radius, or a vertebral fragility fracture identified on x-ray, CT, MRI or vertebral fracture assessment. Other criteria include serum calcium more than 1.0 mg/dL above the upper limit of normal, 24-hour urine calcium above 400 mg/day, and reduced eGFR. This patient meets surgical criteria on two counts, so observation is inappropriate.

references.title: Guidelines for the Management of Asymptomatic Primary Hyperparathyroidism: Summary Statement from the Fourth International Workshop

questions.stem: A 44-year-old woman with autoimmune primary adrenal insufficiency and positive 21-hydroxylase antibodies asks about her long-term replacement regimen. Which of the following best describes the recommended adult replacement regimen?

options.A: Hydrocortisone 20-30 mg given once each morning, with no mineralocorticoid replacement
options.B: Dexamethasone 0.75 mg daily plus fludrocortisone 0.1 mg daily, because dexamethasone has the longest half-life
options.C: Prednisolone 5 mg daily alone once the morning cortisol is within the reference range
options.D: Fludrocortisone (median 0.1 mg) once daily plus hydrocortisone 15-25 mg per day (or cortisone acetate 20-35 mg per day) given in two to three daily doses, with stress-dose education, a steroid card and parenteral emergency cover
options.E: Replacement can be stopped permanently once the patient feels well, with annual reassessment

questions.explanation: The Endocrine Society clinical practice guideline for primary adrenal insufficiency recommends once-daily fludrocortisone (median 0.1 mg) and hydrocortisone 15-25 mg/day or cortisone acetate 20-35 mg/day in two to three daily doses for adults. Patients must be educated about stress dosing and given a steroid card and a glucocorticoid preparation for parenteral emergency administration. Replacement is lifelong, and single daily dosing or dexamethasone-based regimens are not recommended.

references.title: Diagnosis and Treatment of Primary Adrenal Insufficiency: An Endocrine Society Clinical Practice Guideline

questions.stem: A 9-year-old child with homozygous sickle cell disease (HbSS) attends routine follow-up in a low- to middle-income setting; the peripheral blood smear is shown. There has been no prior stroke or transient ischaemic attack. According to the American Society of Hematology 2020 guidelines for cerebrovascular disease in sickle cell disease, which strategy is recommended for primary stroke prevention?

image.alt: Giemsa-stained peripheral blood smear showing sickle-shaped red cells and target cells
image.caption: Peripheral blood smear demonstrating sickle erythrocytes in homozygous sickle cell disease
image.source: Wikimedia Commons – File:Sickle Cell Blood Smear.JPG (Keith Chambers, CC BY-SA 3.0)

options.A: Transcranial Doppler ultrasound screening, with hydroxyurea used for primary stroke prevention in children with HbSS or HbS beta-zero thalassaemia
options.B: Routine prophylactic chronic transfusion for every child with HbSS irrespective of Doppler velocities
options.C: Screening only after the first clinical stroke has occurred, because silent infarcts are not actionable
options.D: Carotid endarterectomy based on carotid intima-media thickness measurement
options.E: Primary intracranial haemorrhage prophylaxis with low-dose aspirin in all children

questions.explanation: One of the three immediately practice-changing recommendations of the ASH 2020 cerebrovascular guideline is the use of transcranial Doppler ultrasound screening and hydroxyurea for primary stroke prevention in children with HbSS and HbS beta-zero thalassaemia living in low- to middle-income settings. The guideline also supports MRI of the brain without sedation to detect silent cerebral infarcts and surveillance for neurodevelopmental problems. Screening only after stroke occurs cannot provide primary prevention.

references.title: American Society of Hematology 2020 guidelines for sickle cell disease: prevention, diagnosis, and treatment of cerebrovascular disease in children and adults

questions.stem: A 52-year-old woman with newly diagnosed primary immune thrombocytopenia was started on corticosteroids but after 6 weeks her platelet count remains 18 x 10(9)/L with minor mucosal bleeding. She has had no splenectomy. According to the American Society of Hematology guideline update for ITP, which option is recommended next?

options.A: Continue high-dose corticosteroids indefinitely until the count normalises
options.B: Rituximab as the only second-line option, because splenectomy is no longer recommended by ASH
options.C: Splenectomy, which is often appropriate when platelet counts remain below 30 x 10(9)/L after 4 to 6 weeks of medical treatment
options.D: Observation alone, because treatment is indicated only when the count falls below 10 x 10(9)/L
options.E: Immediate high-dose intravenous immunoglobulin followed by chronic transfusion support

questions.explanation: The ASH ITP guideline update advises that splenectomy is often appropriate if platelet counts remain below 30,000 after 4 to 6 weeks of medical treatment, and gives a grade 1B recommendation for splenectomy in adults who fail corticosteroid therapy. Rituximab may be considered for patients who have failed at least one other therapy or who are not splenectomy candidates, and thrombopoietin receptor agonists for those who have failed one line of therapy. Observation alone is inappropriate with ongoing bleeding.

references.title: Evidence-based management of immune thrombocytopenia: ASH guideline update

questions.stem: A haemodynamically stable 71-year-old man with anaemia of chronic disease has a haemoglobin concentration of 68 g/L and no major haemorrhage, acute coronary syndrome or regular transfusion requirement. According to NICE guidance on blood transfusion, which transfusion strategy is appropriate?

options.A: Use a restrictive threshold, transfusing at a haemoglobin below 70 g/L and targeting 70-90 g/L after transfusion
options.B: Transfuse at any haemoglobin below 100 g/L to reduce hospital stay
options.C: Transfuse at 80 g/L for every patient regardless of cardiovascular status
options.D: Wait until haemoglobin falls below 50 g/L before transfusing

questions.explanation: NICE NG24 recommends restrictive red blood cell transfusion thresholds for people who do not have major haemorrhage, acute coronary syndrome or a need for regular transfusion for chronic anaemia, using a threshold of 70 g/L with a post-transfusion target of 70-90 g/L. A higher threshold of 80 g/L with a target of 80-100 g/L applies specifically to people with acute coronary syndrome. Single-unit transfusions should be considered in stable patients.

references.title: Blood transfusion - Red blood cell transfusion

questions.stem: A 60-year-old man with acute myeloid leukaemia has a platelet count of 30 x 10(9)/L and is scheduled for insertion of a central venous catheter. He has no active bleeding. According to NICE guidance, which platelet transfusion strategy should be considered?

options.A: No platelet transfusion, because prophylaxis is only given during active haemorrhage
options.B: A prophylactic platelet transfusion to raise the platelet count above 50 x 10(9)/L before the procedure
options.C: A prophylactic transfusion only if the count is below 20 x 10(9)/L at any time
options.D: A transfusion to raise the count above 100 x 10(9)/L for every invasive procedure
options.E: Routine transfusion to a target of 150 x 10(9)/L to prevent delayed bleeding

questions.explanation: NICE NG24 recommends considering prophylactic platelet transfusions to raise the platelet count above 50 x 10(9)/L in people having invasive procedures or surgery, with a higher threshold of 50-75 x 10(9)/L for those at high risk of bleeding. Counts of 10-20 x 10(9)/L are the usual threshold for prophylaxis against spontaneous bleeding in haematological malignancy, not for procedures. Higher targets are not routinely required.

references.title: Blood transfusion - Platelet transfusion

questions.stem: A 26-year-old man with sickle cell disease presents on day one of an acute painful episode in the lower back. His pain is severe and he has received no analgesia before arrival. Which of the following analgesic strategies is recommended?

options.A: Oral ibuprofen alone and discharge home with a follow-up in one week
options.B: Non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs alone until the pain score falls below 3
options.C: Intravenous paracetamol only, avoiding opioids unless the episode persists beyond 48 hours
options.D: A bolus dose of a strong opioid by a suitable route in line with local protocols, plus regular paracetamol and non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs unless contraindicated
options.E: Codeine-only analgesia because strong opioids are reserved for renal colic

questions.explanation: NICE CG134 (sickle cell disease: managing acute painful episodes in hospital) advises a bolus dose of a strong opioid by a suitable route for all patients presenting with severe pain, along with regular paracetamol and NSAIDs in addition to the opioid unless contraindicated. A weak opioid may be considered as an alternative to a strong opioid only for moderate pain in patients who have not taken analgesia before presentation. NSAIDs should be avoided in the third trimester of pregnancy.

references.title: Sickle cell disease: managing acute painful episodes in hospital - Recommendations

questions.stem: A 45-year-old woman is found to have iron deficiency anaemia with no obvious cause on history or examination. She is being investigated for possible colorectal malignancy in the community. Which test should be offered to guide the urgency of her referral?

options.A: Guaiac-based faecal occult blood testing on three consecutive samples
options.B: Serum ferritin alone, repeated after four weeks of oral iron
options.C: Direct straight-to-test colonoscopy without any faecal assessment
options.D: A quantitative faecal immunochemical test (FIT)

questions.explanation: NICE NG12 recommends offering a quantitative faecal immunochemical test using HM-JACKarc or OC-Sensor to guide referral for suspected colorectal cancer in adults presenting with iron-deficiency anaemia, among other lower gastrointestinal presentations. FIT is used alongside clinical assessment to decide on urgent two-week-wait referral rather than to rule out cancer. Guaiac-based faecal occult blood testing is no longer used for this pathway.

references.title: Suspected cancer: recognition and referral - recommendations organised by site of cancer

questions.stem: A 63-year-old man with non-small cell lung cancer on nivolumab develops grade 3 immune-mediated colitis with more than seven stools per day over baseline and incontinence. Which of the following is the recommended general management approach?

options.A: Continue nivolumab unchanged and start loperamide with dietary modification
options.B: Hold nivolumab and start prednisone 0.5-1 mg/kg/day, tapering over four weeks
options.C: Permanently discontinue nivolumab immediately regardless of symptom resolution
options.D: Hold nivolumab and give high-dose corticosteroids tapered over one week only
options.E: Hold nivolumab and initiate high-dose corticosteroids (prednisone or methylprednisolone 1-2 mg/kg/day) tapered over at least four to six weeks, offering infliximab if there is no improvement after 48 to 72 hours

questions.explanation: The ASCO guideline for immune-related adverse events recommends holding checkpoint inhibitors for grade 3 toxicities and initiating high-dose corticosteroids at prednisone or methylprednisolone 1-2 mg/kg/day, tapered over at least four to six weeks. If symptoms do not improve with 48 to 72 hours of high-dose corticosteroid, infliximab may be offered for some toxicities. Permanent discontinuation is the general rule for grade 4 toxicity, except for endocrinopathies controlled by hormone replacement.

references.title: Management of Immune-Related Adverse Events in Patients Treated With Immune Checkpoint Inhibitor Therapy: American Society of Clinical Oncology Clinical Practice Guideline

questions.stem: A 61-year-old man asks about bowel cancer screening in the UK. He is registered with a general practitioner and has no symptoms. Which of the following correctly describes the current programme?

options.A: He will automatically be sent a faecal immunochemical test (FIT) kit every 2 years from age 50 to 74, with screening continuing after 75 on request
options.B: Screening is offered every 3 years to everyone aged 40 to 74 using a guaiac faecal occult blood test
options.C: Screening consists of flexi-sigmoidoscopy once at age 55 followed by no further testing
options.D: Screening is offered annually to all adults from age 18 using a stool DNA test
options.E: Screening starts only at age 80, because younger adults have negligible risk

questions.explanation: NHS bowel cancer screening uses a faecal immunochemical test sent automatically every 2 years to people aged 50 to 74 who are registered with a GP, and people aged 75 and over can request the test by calling the bowel cancer screening helpline. The programme no longer uses guaiac-based faecal occult blood testing, and there is no annual or whole-population DNA screening programme in the UK.

references.title: Bowel cancer screening

questions.stem: A 66-year-old postmenopausal woman has completed primary surgery and systemic therapy for node-positive invasive breast cancer and has no known bone metastases. She has no contraindication to bisphosphonate therapy. According to NICE guidance, which of the following is recommended?

options.A: No adjuvant bone-directed therapy, because bisphosphonates are only licensed for metastatic disease
options.B: Bisphosphonates only if a follow-up scan shows new bone lesions
options.C: Offer bisphosphonates (zoledronic acid or sodium clodronate) as adjuvant therapy
options.D: Offer bisphosphonates routinely to all premenopausal women with node-negative disease
options.E: Delay bone-directed therapy until the patient develops a fragility fracture

questions.explanation: NICE NG101 recommends offering bisphosphonates (zoledronic acid or sodium clodronate) as adjuvant therapy to postmenopausal women with node-positive invasive breast cancer, and considering them for postmenopausal women with node-negative disease at high risk of recurrence. The intent is adjuvant treatment in the absence of metastatic disease, so waiting for bone lesions or a fracture is incorrect. NICE notes that this use was off-label as at March 2025.

references.title: Early and locally advanced breast cancer: diagnosis and management - Recommendations

questions.stem: A palliative care team is reviewing how adults who are likely to be approaching the end of their life are identified in the community. Which of the following tools does NICE recommend that services use to support this identification?

options.A: CHA2DS2-VASc scoring
options.B: The Gold Standards Framework, the Amber Care Bundle or the Supportive and Palliative Care Indicators Tool (SPICT)
options.C: CURB-65 scoring
options.D: The Glasgow Coma Scale

questions.explanation: NICE NG142 recommends that people managing and delivering services develop systems to identify adults likely to be approaching the end of their life, for example using tools such as the Gold Standards Framework, the Amber Care Bundle or SPICT. This enables practitioners to start advance care planning discussions early and support preferences for place of care and death. The other scores are used for stroke risk, pneumonia severity and consciousness assessment respectively.

references.title: End of life care for adults: service delivery - Recommendations

questions.stem: A 47-year-old woman with active rheumatoid arthritis is seropositive for anti-CCP antibodies and the hand radiograph shown demonstrates periarticular erosions. She is starting conventional synthetic DMARD therapy. Which treatment target should be used?

image.alt: Anteroposterior hand radiograph showing marginal erosions and joint space narrowing of rheumatoid arthritis
image.caption: Hand radiograph demonstrating erosive rheumatoid arthritis

options.A: Low disease activity is an acceptable final target for everyone with rheumatoid arthritis
options.B: Remission should be targeted in people at increased risk of radiological progression, such as those with anti-CCP antibodies or erosions on X-ray
options.C: Symptom control alone, because DMARDs should not be escalated once pain improves
options.D: Normalisation of the erythrocyte sedimentation rate without using a composite disease activity score
options.E: A fixed 6-month course of treatment followed by withdrawal of all DMARDs

questions.explanation: NICE NG100 advises treating active rheumatoid arthritis with the aim of achieving remission, or low disease activity if remission cannot be achieved. For people with an increased risk of radiological progression, defined as the presence of anti-CCP antibodies or erosions on X-ray at baseline, the target should be remission rather than low disease activity. Disease activity using a composite score such as DAS28 should be measured monthly in specialist care until the target is reached.

references.title: Rheumatoid arthritis in adults: management - Recommendations

questions.stem: A 29-year-old woman is being assessed against the 2019 EULAR/ACR classification criteria for systemic lupus erythematosus. Which of the following statements about these criteria is correct?

options.A: A positive antinuclear antibody is not required before applying the criteria
options.B: Patients are classified when they accumulate 10 or more weighted points across clinical and immunological domains
options.C: Only clinical domains contribute points; serological findings are ignored
options.D: Antinuclear antibody is the entry criterion and patients are classified only when they reach at least 10 points
options.E: The criteria were designed to guide treatment decisions rather than classification

questions.explanation: The 2019 EULAR/ACR criteria use antinuclear antibody as an entry criterion, after which seven clinical domains and three immunological domains contribute weighted scores, and patients accumulating at least 10 points are classified as having SLE. In the validation cohort the new criteria achieved a sensitivity of 96.1% and specificity of 93.4%, outperforming ACR 1997 and SLICC 2012 criteria on sensitivity. They are classification criteria, not treatment guidelines.

references.title: 2019 EULAR/ACR Classification Criteria for Systemic Lupus Erythematosus

questions.stem: A 54-year-old man presents with a first episode of acute monoarthritis of the first metatarsophalangeal joint. Joint aspiration is performed. Which serum urate value is used to confirm the diagnosis of gout in a person with compatible symptoms and signs?

options.A: 360 micromol/L (6 mg/dL) or more
options.B: 420 micromol/L (7 mg/dL) or more only if measured during the acute flare
options.C: 540 micromol/L (9 mg/dL) or more
options.D: Any value, because serum urate is normal during all acute flares and is never diagnostic
options.E: Less than 300 micromol/L (5 mg/dL) is required to confirm gout

questions.explanation: NICE NG219 recommends measuring serum urate in people with symptoms and signs of gout to confirm the clinical diagnosis, using a level of 360 micromol/L (6 mg/dL) or more. If the level is below 360 micromol/L during a flare and gout is strongly suspected, the measurement should be repeated at least 2 weeks after the flare has settled. Long-term urate-lowering therapy is then offered using a treat-to-target strategy to eligible patients.

references.title: Gout: diagnosis and management - Recommendations

questions.stem: A 63-year-old woman with painful knee osteoarthritis asks for medication. Examination shows no features of inflammatory arthritis and imaging is not required for diagnosis. Which of the following is in line with NICE guidance?

options.A: Start regular oral paracetamol as first-line pharmacological treatment for knee osteoarthritis
options.B: Offer arthroscopic debridement before any attempt at exercise therapy
options.C: Offer a topical NSAID alongside therapeutic exercise, and do not routinely offer paracetamol or weak opioids
options.D: Start a weak opioid daily until pain resolves completely

questions.explanation: NICE NG226 states that the core treatments for osteoarthritis are therapeutic exercise and weight management where appropriate, with information and support. It recommends offering a topical NSAID to people with knee osteoarthritis, while paracetamol and weak opioids should not be offered routinely unless used infrequently for short-term relief when other treatments are contraindicated, not tolerated or ineffective. Imaging is usually unnecessary to confirm the diagnosis.

references.title: Osteoarthritis in over 16s: diagnosis and management - Recommendations

questions.stem: A 24-year-old man develops generalised urticaria, stridor and hypotension (blood pressure 70/40 mm Hg) within 10 minutes of eating a peanut-containing meal. Intramuscular adrenaline is indicated. Which dose should be given to an adult or teenager?

options.A: 50 micrograms intramuscularly, because smaller doses avoid myocardial ischaemia
options.B: 150 micrograms intramuscularly, the dose used for infants under 6 months
options.C: 500 micrograms (0.5 mg) intramuscularly, that is 0.5 mL of 1 mg/mL adrenaline
options.D: 5 mg intravenously as a bolus to achieve rapid reversal of shock
options.E: 300 micrograms subcutaneously, repeating once after 15 minutes if blood pressure remains low

questions.explanation: Resuscitation Council UK advises that the recommended dose of adrenaline in teenagers and adults is 500 micrograms given intramuscularly, even though most adult auto-injectors deliver a 300 microgram dose. Evidence reviews of anaphylaxis treatment list the adult and over-12-year dose as 500 micrograms IM (0.5 mL of 1 mg/mL adrenaline), with 300 micrograms for 6-12 years and 150 micrograms for 6 months to 6 years. Intravenous adrenaline boluses are not the routine first-line treatment for anaphylaxis.

references.title: Guidance: Anaphylaxis
Evidence update for the treatment of anaphylaxis

questions.stem: A 73-year-old woman attends for vaccination review. According to the UK complete routine immunisation schedule, which of the following correctly describes eligibility for shingles (herpes zoster) vaccination?

options.A: All adults aged 60 and over are offered the vaccine as a single catch-up dose
options.B: Only adults aged 80 and over are eligible, because younger adults have sufficient immunity
options.C: The programme offers live zoster vaccine to everyone aged 40 to 59 regardless of immune status
options.D: Vaccination is restricted to immunocompetent adults aged 70 to 79 only, with no roll-forward cohort
options.E: Individuals turning 65 from 1 September each year, those aged 70 to 79, and those severely immunosuppressed aged 18 or over are eligible for Shingrix

questions.explanation: The current UK schedule lists shingles vaccination for individuals turning 65 from 1 September each year (from 1 September 2023 onwards), for those aged 70 to 79 years, and for those severely immunosuppressed aged 18 years and over, using Shingrix. The schedule is also updated regularly, for example to reflect changes to the shingles programme from 1 September 2025. Eligibility is therefore not limited to a single decade of life.

references.title: Complete routine immunisation schedule from 1 September 2026
Complete routine immunisation schedule

questions.stem: A 4-year-old boy has a history of recurrent severe bacterial skin abscesses and catalase-positive staphylococci, and neutrophil oxidative burst testing is absent, confirming chronic granulomatous disease. According to the IUIS 2022 classification of inborn errors of immunity, into which category does this disorder fall?

options.A: Diseases of immune dysregulation
options.B: Autoinflammatory diseases
options.C: Complement deficiencies
options.D: Congenital defects of phagocytes
options.E: Predominantly antibody deficiencies

questions.explanation: The IUIS 2022 update classifies inborn errors of immunity into 10 tables covering combined immunodeficiencies, combined immunodeficiencies with syndromic features, predominantly antibody deficiencies, diseases of immune dysregulation, congenital defects of phagocytes, defects in intrinsic and innate immunity, autoinflammatory diseases, complement deficiencies, bone marrow failure, and phenocopies, with a total of 485 disorders. Chronic granulomatous disease, a defect of the NADPH oxidase complex, belongs to congenital defects of phagocytes. Complement deficiencies would present with encapsulated bacterial infections or Neisseria infections instead.

references.title: Human Inborn Errors of Immunity: 2022 Update on the Classification from the International Union of Immunological Societies Expert Committee

questions.stem: A 50-year-old man is discharged after kidney transplantation on maintenance therapy with tacrolimus, mycophenolate mofetil and prednisolone. Which of the following best describes the mechanism of action of tacrolimus?

options.A: It inhibits the mammalian target of rapamycin, blocking interleukin-2-driven T-cell proliferation
options.B: It blocks calcineurin, preventing dephosphorylation and nuclear entry of NFAT and thereby reducing interleukin-2 transcription
options.C: It inhibits de novo purine synthesis by blocking inosine monophosphate dehydrogenase
options.D: It blocks the CD28-CD80/CD86 co-stimulatory interaction between T cell and antigen-presenting cell
options.E: It depletes B cells by binding to CD20 and accelerating antibody-dependent cellular cytotoxicity

questions.explanation: Calcineurin inhibitors such as tacrolimus and cyclosporine block calcineurin, so NFAT is not dephosphorylated, cannot enter the nucleus and interleukin-2 transcription falls, reducing T-cell proliferation. Mycophenolate inhibits inosine monophosphate dehydrogenase and thus DNA synthesis, everolimus and sirolimus inhibit mTOR, corticosteroids suppress cytokine production, and belatacept blocks co-stimulation through CD28-CD80/CD86.

references.title: Maintenance Immunosuppression in Kidney Transplantation: A Review of the Current Status and Future Directions

questions.stem: A 24-year-old woman has a sexual partner living with HIV who has a detectable viral load. She does not use condoms consistently and wants to start pre-exposure prophylaxis (PrEP). Which of the following statements about PrEP is correct?

options.A: PrEP can be started without an HIV test because she has no symptoms of HIV infection
options.B: When taken daily, oral PrEP takes about 21 days to reach maximum protection against HIV for receptive vaginal sex and injection drug use
options.C: The on-demand 2-1-1 regimen (2 pills before sex, then one pill 24 and 48 hours after) is approved by the FDA and routinely recommended by CDC
options.D: PrEP has known interactions with combined hormonal contraception, so an additional contraceptive method is always required
options.E: Once PrEP is started, routine follow-up HIV testing is unnecessary because PrEP also treats undiagnosed infection

questions.explanation: CDC states that daily oral PrEP reaches maximum protection at about 7 days of use for receptive anal sex and about 21 days for receptive vaginal sex and injection drug use. An HIV test must be performed before starting PrEP to confirm the person does not have HIV, and routine follow-up HIV testing is required while on PrEP. There are no known interactions between PrEP and hormone-based birth control methods. The 2-1-1 on-demand schedule has evidence only for gay and bisexual men having anal sex, is not FDA approved and is not recommended by CDC.

references.title: Preventing HIV with PrEP

questions.stem: A 28-year-old woman is identified as a close household contact of a smear-positive case of pulmonary tuberculosis. She is asymptomatic, her chest radiograph shows no active disease and assessment rules out active TB. She is under 35 years old with normal liver function and no HIV infection. According to NICE guidance, which regimen should be offered to treat her latent tuberculosis infection?

options.A: Two months of rifampicin, isoniazid, pyrazinamide and ethambutol followed by one month of isoniazid and rifampicin
options.B: Six months of rifampicin alone
options.C: Three months of isoniazid (with pyridoxine) plus rifampicin, or six months of isoniazid (with pyridoxine)
options.D: Nine months of isoniazid alone as the only acceptable regimen for all age groups
options.E: No drug treatment; repeat an interferon-gamma release assay annually instead

questions.explanation: For people aged under 65 years with latent TB who are close contacts of infectious pulmonary or laryngeal TB, NICE NG33 offers a choice of 3 months of isoniazid with pyridoxine plus rifampicin, or 6 months of isoniazid with pyridoxine. In people younger than 35 years the 3-month dual regimen is preferred when hepatotoxicity is a concern after assessing liver function and risk factors, and the 6-month isoniazid regimen is used when rifamycin interactions are a concern (for example with HIV treatment). Active TB must always be excluded before treating latent infection.

references.title: Tuberculosis: recommendations

questions.topic: Suspected bacterial meningitis - antibiotics before transfer
questions.stem: A 32-year-old man is strongly suspected to have bacterial meningitis at a district hospital (fever, headache, neck stiffness and confusion). He must be transferred to a tertiary centre, but a clinically significant delay in transfer is likely because no ambulance is immediately available. According to NICE NG240, what should be done before transfer?

options.A: Arrange emergency transfer and give intravenous or intramuscular ceftriaxone or benzylpenicillin outside hospital because transfer will be significantly delayed
options.B: Delay transfer until a lumbar puncture has been performed at the district hospital
options.C: Give oral amoxicillin and re-assess after 24 hours before deciding on transfer
options.D: Withhold all antibiotics until the patient arrives at the tertiary centre

questions.explanation: NICE NG240 recommends transferring people with suspected bacterial meningitis to hospital as an emergency and not delaying transfer merely to give antibiotics. However, if there is likely to be a clinically significant delay in transfer, intravenous or intramuscular ceftriaxone or benzylpenicillin should be given outside hospital; the same applies as soon as possible for strongly suspected meningococcal disease unless this would delay transfer. Antibiotics must not be given outside hospital only if there is severe allergy to both ceftriaxone and benzylpenicillin.

references.title: Meningitis (bacterial) and meningococcal disease: recognition, diagnosis and management - recommendations

questions.topic: Severe Plasmodium falciparum malaria - parenteral artesunate
questions.stem: A 28-year-old man returns from Nigeria with high fever, jaundice, vomiting and impaired consciousness. Thick and thin blood films confirm Plasmodium falciparum malaria with high parasitaemia; the blood smear is shown. He is unable to take oral medication. Which of the following is the most appropriate treatment?

image.alt: Microscopic blood smear showing crescent-shaped Plasmodium falciparum gametocytes
image.caption: Blood smear demonstrating Plasmodium falciparum gametocytes
image.source: Wikimedia Commons - File:Plasmodium falciparum 01.png (Public domain, CDC/PHIL)

options.A: Oral artemether-lumefantrine alone, since all uncomplicated and severe malaria can be managed orally once vomiting stops
options.B: Intravenous quinine as first-line treatment, with artesunate reserved only if quinine is contraindicated
options.C: Intravenous or intramuscular artesunate for at least 24 hours and until he can tolerate oral medication, then complete a 3-day course of an artemisinin-based combination therapy (ACT)
options.D: A single intramuscular dose of artesunate followed immediately by chloroquine to clear the infection
options.E: Stop parenteral treatment as soon as parasitaemia falls below 1% and give a single dose of primaquine as the definitive cure

questions.explanation: WHO recommends treating severe malaria in adults and children (including pregnant women) with intravenous or intramuscular artesunate for at least 24 hours and until the patient can tolerate oral medication; treatment is then completed with 3 days of an ACT. Children under 20 kg should receive a higher dose (3 mg/kg per dose rather than 2.4 mg/kg). If artesunate is unavailable, artemether is preferred over quinine. Chloroquine is ineffective for falciparum malaria in most endemic areas, and primaquine is used for transmission blocking or radical cure of P. vivax/ovale, not to complete severe malaria therapy.

references.title: WHO guidelines for malaria

questions.stem: A healthy, unvaccinated 2-year-old girl is brought to the clinic 32 hours after close contact with a child who has confirmed measles. She has no immunodeficiency and has not yet developed symptoms. Which of the following is the most appropriate post-exposure prophylaxis?

options.A: MMR vaccine now, because it can be given within 72 hours of initial exposure (immunoglobulin would be reserved for those unable to receive MMR)
options.B: Intramuscular immunoglobulin only, because MMR vaccine is not effective as post-exposure prophylaxis
options.C: No prophylaxis is possible because the 72-hour window has already passed
options.D: MMR vaccine together with immunoglobulin at the same visit to maximise protection
options.E: Oral aciclovir prophylaxis for 7 days

questions.explanation: CDC advises offering post-exposure prophylaxis to susceptible contacts: MMR vaccine if administered within 72 hours of initial measles exposure, or immunoglobulin if administered within 6 days (0.5 mL/kg intramuscularly for IMIG). MMR and immunoglobulin must not be given simultaneously because this invalidates the vaccine. For a healthy, immunocompetent child seen at 32 hours, MMR within the 72-hour window is the appropriate choice; immunoglobulin is used for people who cannot receive vaccine (for example severe immunodeficiency or infants for whom vaccine is not licensed).

references.title: Measles vaccine recommendations for healthcare professionals

questions.topic: Infective endocarditis - antibiotic prophylaxis for dental procedures
questions.stem: A 66-year-old man with a mechanical mitral valve prosthesis is scheduled for scaling and root canal treatment. He has no signs of infection. According to the 2023 ESC endocarditis guidelines, which of the following is the most appropriate approach to infective endocarditis prophylaxis?

options.A: No antibiotic prophylaxis, because endocarditis prophylaxis is not recommended for any cardiac patient undergoing dental procedures
options.B: Amoxicillin 2 g orally as a single dose 30-60 minutes before the dental procedure
options.C: Clindamycin 600 mg orally four times daily for 7 days, because clindamycin has the best safety profile for prophylaxis
options.D: Amoxicillin 2 g three times daily for 7 days to cover oral flora
options.E: Prophylaxis only if the patient develops a fever after the procedure, with a blood culture taken first

questions.explanation: The 2023 ESC guidelines recommend antibiotic prophylaxis in patients at high risk of infective endocarditis (including those with previous IE and prosthetic valves) undergoing at-risk dental procedures that involve manipulation of the gingival or periapical region, such as extractions, periodontal surgery, implant surgery and scaling/root canal procedures. The standard adult regimen is amoxicillin 2 g orally as a single dose 30-60 minutes before the procedure. Clindamycin is not recommended for prophylaxis because of its risk of adverse events, mainly Clostridioides difficile infection. No prophylaxis is recommended for patients at intermediate or unknown risk.

references.title: 2023 ESC Guidelines for the management of infective endocarditis

questions.topic: Antimicrobial resistance - WHO bacterial priority pathogens list
questions.stem: An infectious diseases team is prioritising research and development of new antimicrobials using the WHO Bacterial Priority Pathogens List (BPPL) 2024. Which of the following pathogens is classified in the critical priority group?

options.A: Acinetobacter baumannii, carbapenem-resistant
options.B: Staphylococcus aureus, methicillin-resistant
options.C: Pseudomonas aeruginosa, carbapenem-resistant
options.D: Enterococcus faecium, vancomycin-resistant
options.E: Neisseria gonorrhoeae, third-generation cephalosporin- and/or fluoroquinolone-resistant

questions.explanation: The WHO BPPL 2024 groups pathogens into critical, high and medium priorities across 15 families. The critical priority group comprises carbapenem-resistant Acinetobacter baumannii, third-generation cephalosporin-resistant Enterobacterales, carbapenem-resistant Enterobacterales, and rifampicin-resistant Mycobacterium tuberculosis. Methicillin-resistant S. aureus, carbapenem-resistant P. aeruginosa, vancomycin-resistant E. faecium and multidrug-resistant N. gonorrhoeae are all in the high priority group.

references.title: WHO bacterial priority pathogens list, 2024

questions.stem: An emergency department nurse sustains a percutaneous needlestick injury from a patient with known HIV infection. By the time she presents for assessment, 80 hours have elapsed since the exposure. She has no symptoms. Which of the following is the most appropriate management?

options.A: Start a 28-day course of HIV post-exposure prophylaxis immediately, since occupational exposure has no time limit
options.B: Start post-exposure prophylaxis now but shorten the course to 7 days because the exposure is old
options.C: Start pre-exposure prophylaxis instead, which remains effective at any time after exposure
options.D: Delay post-exposure prophylaxis until the source patient's CD4 count is available
options.E: Do not start post-exposure prophylaxis because it must be started within 72 hours of exposure; take a baseline HIV test and arrange follow-up testing

questions.explanation: CDC states that PEP must be started within 72 hours (3 days) after a possible HIV exposure, that the sooner PEP is started the better, and that a prescribed PEP course is taken daily for 28 days. At 80 hours the exposure is outside the 72-hour window, so PEP should not be started; instead a baseline HIV test with appropriate follow-up testing and counselling is indicated. PrEP is for ongoing risk before exposure, not for treatment after an exposure.

references.title: Preventing HIV with PEP

questions.stem: A 36-hour-old term infant (39 weeks' gestation) is shown. He is clinically well, is being exclusively breastfed, and his total serum bilirubin is 30 micromol/L below the age-specific phototherapy threshold on the NICE threshold table. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step?

image.alt: Newborn infant with visible jaundice of the skin
image.caption: Term newborn with clinically apparent jaundice
image.source: Wikimedia Commons - File:Jaundice in newborn.jpg (Public domain, CDC)

options.A: Start phototherapy immediately because visible jaundice always requires treatment in the first 48 hours
options.B: Repeat the bilirubin measurement within 18 hours because he has a risk factor (intended exclusive breastfeeding) and the level is within 50 micromol/L of the threshold
options.C: Repeat the bilirubin measurement within 24 hours, since this interval applies to all well babies
options.D: No repeat measurement is needed because the level is below the phototherapy threshold

questions.explanation: NICE CG98 advises that in clinically well babies aged 38 weeks or more and over 24 hours old whose bilirubin is below but within 50 micromol/L of the phototherapy threshold, measurement is repeated within 18 hours if there are risk factors (a sibling who needed phototherapy for jaundice, or a mother who intends to exclusively breastfeed) and within 24 hours if there are no risk factors. Phototherapy must not be started when bilirubin does not exceed the threshold. If the level is more than 50 micromol/L below the threshold, routine repeat measurement is not needed.

references.title: Neonatal jaundice: recommendations

questions.stem: During a bronchiolitis ward round, two infants are assessed. A 3-week-old and a 4-month-old both have clinically diagnosed bronchiolitis and a persistent oxygen saturation of 91% while breathing air. Neither has an underlying health condition. According to NICE NG9, which of the following is correct?

options.A: The 4-month-old should start oxygen because the treatment threshold is 92% for all infants under 1 year
