options.B: Neither infant needs oxygen, and both can be managed at home with safety-netting advice
options.C: Both infants should start oxygen because both saturations are below 92%
options.D: The 3-week-old should start oxygen (treatment threshold is persistently below 92% for babies under 6 weeks), whereas the 4-month-old should not (threshold is persistently below 90% from 6 weeks onwards), although he warrants admission assessment
options.E: The 4-month-old should start oxygen while the 3-week-old should not, because the threshold rises with age

questions.explanation: NICE NG9 recommendation 1.4.4 (2021) says to give oxygen supplementation if oxygen saturation is persistently less than 90% in children aged 6 weeks and over, or persistently less than 92% in babies under 6 weeks or children of any age with underlying health conditions. Thus the 3-week-old at 91% requires oxygen while the 4-month-old does not on saturation alone (though persistent saturation below 92% in air is a criterion for referral/admission, and bronchiolitis care includes feeding and hydration support). Bronchiolitis should not be treated with salbutamol, antibiotics, corticosteroids or routine chest radiography.

references.title: Bronchiolitis: recommendations

questions.topic: Fever under 5s - traffic light risk stratification
questions.stem: A 14-month-old child is assessed in the emergency department with fever. Which one of the following features places the child in the high-risk (red) group of the NICE NG143 traffic light system for risk of serious illness?

options.A: Pallor of the skin, lips or tongue reported by the parent
options.B: Waking only with prolonged stimulation
options.C: A weak, high-pitched or continuous cry
options.D: Nasal flaring with a respiratory rate of 42 breaths per minute
options.E: Reduced feeding with normal activity, colour and interaction

questions.explanation: NICE NG143 recognises a weak, high-pitched or continuous cry as a high-risk (red) feature, along with pale/mottled/ashen/blue skin, no response to social cues, not waking or not staying awake when roused, grunting, respiratory rate above 60 per minute, moderate or severe chest indrawing, reduced skin turgor and a bulging fontanelle. Pallor reported by a carer, waking only with prolonged stimulation, and tachypnoea/nasal flaring at this age (amber threshold is above 40 breaths per minute for children over 12 months) are intermediate (amber) risk features. Management is directed by the risk category, with low risk managed in the community with safety-netting advice.

references.title: Fever in under 5s: diagnosis and management - recommendations

questions.stem: A 4-year-old presents for catch-up immunisation. He received only 3 of 5 DTaP doses (the last dose was 2 years ago) and a single dose of MMR at 15 months. His mother asks whether the long interval means everything must be started again. According to the CDC/ACIP child and adolescent catch-up schedule, which of the following is correct?

options.A: Continue the existing series and give catch-up doses at the earliest opportunity using the minimum intervals in Table 2, because a vaccine series does not need to be restarted regardless of the time elapsed between doses
options.B: Restart the DTaP series from dose 1 because more than 12 months have elapsed since the previous dose
options.C: Treat the MMR dose at 15 months as invalid and restart MMR as a new two-dose primary series
options.D: Withhold all catch-up doses until the routine adolescent visit at 11-12 years
options.E: Give each vaccine only after observing a 1-month interval between different vaccine products

questions.explanation: CDC's catch-up immunisation schedule states that a vaccine series does not need to be restarted, regardless of the time elapsed between doses, and that for those who fall behind or start late, catch-up vaccination should be provided at the earliest opportunity using the minimum intervals in Table 2 (for example 4 weeks between DTaP doses and 4 weeks between MMR doses). Remaining doses are simply completed according to the catch-up schedule; asymptomatic children do not need serology, and there is no requirement to restart a partially completed series.

references.title: Catch-up immunization schedule for children and adolescents

questions.stem: A 7-year-old girl has had frequent typical absence seizures for 4 months with a normal neurological examination and a 3 Hz generalised spike-and-wave EEG. There are no other seizure types. Which of the following is the first-line treatment according to NICE NG217?

options.A: Carbamazepine, because broad-spectrum antiseizure medication is preferred for all childhood epilepsies
options.B: Lamotrigine as first-line monotherapy for isolated absence seizures
options.C: Sodium valproate as first-line monotherapy for isolated absence seizures
options.D: Ethosuximide as first-line treatment
options.E: Levetiracetam as first-line monotherapy for isolated absence seizures

questions.explanation: NICE NG217 recommendation 5.3.1 advises offering ethosuximide as first-line treatment for absence seizures (including childhood absence epilepsy). If first-line treatment fails, lamotrigine, levetiracetam or sodium valproate are offered as second-line monotherapy or add-on treatment (with MHRA safety measures for valproate). Carbamazepine, phenytoin, oxcarbazepine and other listed drugs can exacerbate absence seizures. Sodium valproate is considered first-line only when absence seizures occur together with other seizure types or there is a risk of these.

references.title: Epilepsies in children, young people and adults - treating epileptic seizures

questions.stem: A woman attends her antenatal clinic at 27 weeks of gestation and asks when she will be offered the RSV vaccine. According to the UK (GOV.UK/UKHSA) RSV vaccination programme for pregnant women, which of the following is correct?

options.A: She should be offered the vaccine from 12 weeks of gestation, in her first pregnancy only
options.B: She should be offered a single dose at 36 weeks of gestation, once in a lifetime
options.C: A single dose should be offered from 28 weeks of gestation in every pregnancy, ideally in week 28 or soon after
options.D: She should be offered the vaccine at any time in the third trimester, but only if she has not previously received it in another pregnancy

questions.explanation: Since 1 September 2024, the UK programme offers a single dose of RSV vaccine (Abrysvo) to every pregnant woman from week 28 of each pregnancy, ideally in week 28 or soon after so that high antibody levels can be transferred across the placenta, including if the baby is born prematurely. Vaccination is offered year-round, not only in the first pregnancy, and can be given up to delivery if missed; the whooping cough vaccine is given earlier, around 20 weeks, and influenza vaccine at any stage.

references.title: RSV vaccination of pregnant women for infant protection: information for healthcare practitioners

questions.topic: Suspected sepsis in under 16s - high-risk management
questions.stem: A 10-year-old boy presents with fever, mottling and tachycardia. He meets one or more high-risk criteria for sepsis, and venous lactate is 4.4 mmol/L. Antibiotics have not yet been given. Which of the following is the most appropriate management according to NICE NG254?

options.A: Give a broad-spectrum antimicrobial within 3 hours after a second senior review, unless the lactate normalises
options.B: Obtain blood cultures and CRP only, and start antibiotics if CRP rises above 100 mg/L at 24 hours
options.C: Give intravenous antibiotics immediately, but withhold fluids unless the systolic blood pressure is low
options.D: Give an intravenous fluid bolus without delay (within 1 hour), give a broad-spectrum antimicrobial within 1 hour of identifying the high-risk criteria, and refer to a critical care specialist or team
options.E: Start inotropes immediately without a fluid bolus or antibiotics because the lactate is over 4 mmol/L

questions.explanation: NICE NG254 advises that for people under 16 meeting high-risk criteria for sepsis, a broad-spectrum antimicrobial is given without delay within 1 hour (if not already given), alongside urgent senior assessment and venous blood tests including blood gas, lactate and blood culture. For children under 12 with high-risk criteria and lactate over 4 mmol/L, an intravenous fluid bolus is given without delay within 1 hour and a critical care specialist or team is referred to review management, including central venous access and initiation of inotropes or vasopressors if needed. For community-acquired sepsis in under-16s (excluding neonates), ceftriaxone is the recommended empirical choice.

references.title: Suspected sepsis in under 16s: recognition, diagnosis and early management - managing suspected sepsis

questions.stem: A 32-year-old woman at 34 weeks of gestation has severe pre-eclampsia: BP 178/112 mmHg, severe headache, visual scotomata and epigastric pain. She is in a critical care setting and has just had an eclamptic fit. Which of the following is the most appropriate treatment?

options.A: Give intravenous magnesium sulfate 6 g as a bolus followed by 2 g/hour for 24 hours, and treat the blood pressure with oral methyldopa titrated over 48 hours
options.B: Treat the severe hypertension immediately with labetalol (oral or intravenous), oral nifedipine or intravenous hydralazine, and give magnesium sulfate 4 g intravenously over 5-15 minutes followed by an infusion of 1 g/hour for 24 hours
options.C: Give dexamethasone to treat the features of HELLP syndrome and delay antihypertensive treatment until after delivery
options.D: Perform vigorous intravenous volume expansion before giving any antihypertensive drug
options.E: Withhold treatment of severe hypertension until the blood pressure exceeds 160/110 mmHg on two consecutive readings over 4 hours

questions.explanation: NICE NG133 states that women with severe hypertension in critical care during pregnancy or after birth are treated immediately with labetalol (oral or intravenous), oral nifedipine, or intravenous hydralazine, with response monitored to confirm the fall in blood pressure. Magnesium sulfate for eclampsia uses the Collaborative Eclampsia Trial regimen: 4 g IV over 5-15 minutes then 1 g/hour for 24 hours (continued 24 hours after the last fit), with a further 2-4 g for recurrent fits. Dexamethasone or betamethasone must not be used to treat HELLP syndrome, and volume expansion is not used in severe pre-eclampsia unless hydralazine is the antenatal antihypertensive (limited to 500 mL crystalloid with the first IV dose).

references.title: Hypertension in pregnancy: recommendations

questions.stem: A birthing centre in a low-resource setting has an unreliable electricity supply, and the oxytocin cold chain cannot be consistently maintained. The WHO consolidated PPH guidelines (2025) are being used to write the local protocol for prevention of postpartum haemorrhage. Which of the following is correct?

options.A: Oxytocin 10 IU intramuscularly should still be used as the first choice regardless of cold-chain status
options.B: Ergometrine is the recommended uterotonic of choice for all births when oxytocin cannot be refrigerated
options.C: Misoprostol 800 micrograms rectally is the preferred alternative to oxytocin in all settings
options.D: No uterotonic is needed; active management of the third stage should rely on fundal massage alone
options.E: Heat-stable carbetocin 100 micrograms intramuscularly or intravenously is the recommended choice when the oxytocin cold chain cannot be consistently maintained, with misoprostol 400 or 600 micrograms orally as an alternative if heat-stable carbetocin is unavailable

questions.explanation: WHO's 2025 consolidated PPH guidelines recommend a quality-assured uterotonic for prevention of PPH in the third stage of labour for all births, using only oxytocin, carbetocin or misoprostol: oxytocin 10 IU IM/IV is the agent of choice when options are available (IV route preferred over IM when IV access exists, given slowly over 1-2 minutes); heat-stable carbetocin 100 micrograms IM/IV is recommended where the oxytocin cold chain cannot be consistently maintained; if it is unavailable, misoprostol 400 or 600 micrograms orally can be used, including by community health workers where skilled personnel and injectable uterotonics are not available.

references.title: Consolidated guidelines for the prevention, diagnosis and treatment of postpartum haemorrhage

questions.stem: A 29-year-old woman is diagnosed with gestational diabetes at 24 weeks of gestation. Her fasting plasma glucose at diagnosis is 7.4 mmol/L. She has no other complications of pregnancy. According to NICE NG3, which of the following is the most appropriate management?

options.A: Give diet and exercise advice for 1-2 weeks first, then start metformin if glucose targets are still not met
options.B: Start metformin monotherapy and review glucose control after 4 weeks
options.C: Offer immediate treatment with insulin (with or without metformin) together with diet and exercise changes
options.D: Arrange immediate caesarean section because of the risk of macrosomia
options.E: No pharmacological treatment; repeat the oral glucose tolerance test at 32 weeks

questions.explanation: NICE NG3 recommends offering immediate treatment with insulin, with or without metformin and diet and exercise changes, to women with gestational diabetes whose fasting plasma glucose is 7.0 mmol/L or above at diagnosis. For fasting levels of 6.0-6.9 mmol/L with complications such as macrosomia or hydramnios, immediate insulin with or without metformin is considered; otherwise diet and exercise are trialled for 1-2 weeks with metformin added if targets are not met. Glucose targets are fasting below 5.3 mmol/L, 1 hour post-meal below 7.8 mmol/L or 2 hours below 6.4 mmol/L, and insulin is offered if targets cannot be met or are unacceptable to the woman.

references.title: Diabetes in pregnancy: recommendations

questions.stem: A 26-year-old woman asks about the routine cervical screening programme in the UK. According to the UK National Screening Committee recommendation, which of the following is correct?

options.A: Screen with cervical cytology every 3 years from age 21 to 65
options.B: Screen with human papillomavirus (HPV) testing every 3 years from age 30 to 60
options.C: Offer an annual cervical smear test from age 25 onwards
options.D: Offer screening with HPV primary testing every 5 years from age 25 to 64

questions.explanation: The UK NSC recommends that cervical screening is offered to women aged 25 to 64 every 5 years using testing for high-risk human papillomavirus as the primary test, so that HPV infection and cervical abnormalities are detected early; screening starts at age 25, not 21. Risk-stratified recall (for example 12-month surveillance for those who are HPV positive with negative cytology) applies to test results rather than changing the routine 5-yearly invitation interval, and the programme is under ongoing review, including evaluation of self-sampling.

references.title: UK NSC screening recommendation for cervical cancer

questions.stem: A 33-year-old woman is stable and pain-free. Transvaginal ultrasound confirms an unruptured tubal ectopic pregnancy with an adnexal mass of 40 mm, no visible heartbeat and no intrauterine pregnancy. Serum hCG is 1,700 IU/L. She wishes to preserve fertility. According to NICE NG126, which of the following is the most appropriate management?

options.A: Offer systemic methotrexate as the definitive treatment, since she is clinically stable and pain-free
options.B: Offer expectant management with hCG repeats on days 2, 4 and 7, because hCG is below 2,000 IU/L
options.C: Review again in 2 weeks with a repeat ultrasound and no treatment in the interim
options.D: Perform emergency laparotomy with hysterectomy to prevent rupture
options.E: Offer surgical management (for example laparoscopic salpingectomy or salpingostomy), because methotrexate and expectant management criteria are not met

questions.explanation: NICE NG126 offers systemic methotrexate only for unruptured tubal ectopics with an adnexal mass smaller than 35 mm, no visible heartbeat, serum hCG below 1,500 IU/L, no significant pain, no intrauterine pregnancy and the ability to return for follow-up. Expectant management is offered when hCG is 1,000 IU/L or less (and considered between 1,000 and 1,500 IU/L) with a mass under 35 mm and no heartbeat. With a 40 mm mass and hCG of 1,700 IU/L neither medical nor expectant criteria are met, so surgical management is indicated; salpingectomy or salpingostomy is chosen laparoscopically according to clinical findings, tubal status and patient preference, with fertility considerations discussed.

references.title: Ectopic pregnancy and miscarriage: management of tubal ectopic pregnancy

questions.stem: A woman is 4 weeks postpartum and had a deep vein thrombosis during this pregnancy (so she has postpartum status plus another venous thromboembolism risk factor). She requests depot medroxyprogesterone acetate (DMPA) for contraception. According to UKMEC 2025, which of the following is correct?

options.A: DMPA is UKMEC category 1, so there is no restriction on use
options.B: DMPA is UKMEC category 2, and the advantages generally outweigh the disadvantages
options.C: DMPA is UKMEC category 4 and is absolutely contraindicated
options.D: DMPA is UKMEC category 3 (generally not recommended) for postpartum women with other VTE risk factors, and a more suitable method should be offered
options.E: UKMEC 2025 retains category 2 for this situation, so DMPA can be started without further assessment

questions.explanation: In UKMEC 2025 the category for DMPA in women who are postpartum with other risk factors for VTE was raised from 2 to 3, meaning it is generally not recommended and another method is preferred. UKMEC 2025 introduced new conditions (multiple sclerosis, chronic kidney disease, sickle cell trait and multiple VTE risk factors), changed several DMPA categories where VTE risk is increased (for example BMI over 35 changed from 1 to 2, and known thrombogenic mutations and positive antiphospholipid antibodies from 2 to 3), and updated guidance on hypertension, HIV and anxiety/mood disorders.

references.title: UK Medical Eligibility Criteria for Contraceptive Use (UKMEC) 2025
references.org: College of Sexual and Reproductive Healthcare (CoSRH/FSRH)

questions.stem: A pregnant woman asks whether she should take low-dose aspirin to prevent pre-eclampsia. According to NICE NG133, which of the following women should be advised to take aspirin 75-150 mg daily from 12 weeks until the birth of the baby?

options.A: A 28-year-old primigravida with a BMI of 24 kg/m2 and no other risk factors
options.B: A 35-year-old woman with chronic hypertension
options.C: A 30-year-old woman whose only risk factor is nulliparity
options.D: A 26-year-old woman with migraine but no other risk factors

questions.explanation: NICE NG133 advises aspirin 75-150 mg daily from 12 weeks until birth for women at high risk of pre-eclampsia: hypertensive disease in a previous pregnancy, chronic kidney disease, autoimmune disease such as systemic lupus erythematosus or antiphospholipid syndrome, type 1 or type 2 diabetes, or chronic hypertension. It is also advised for women with more than one moderate risk factor (nulliparity, age 40 or older, pregnancy interval over 10 years, BMI 35 kg/m2 or more at first visit, family history of pre-eclampsia, or multi-fetal pregnancy). A single moderate risk factor alone does not qualify.

references.title: Hypertension in pregnancy: recommendations

questions.topic: Cutaneous melanoma - staging and excision margins
questions.stem: An excision biopsy of a pigmented lesion on the back shows melanoma with a Breslow thickness of 1.4 mm, no ulceration, a mitotic rate of 1/mm2 and no lymphovascular invasion. Clinical examination of the nodes is normal and the biopsy was taken with a 2 mm margin. According to NICE NG14, which of the following is the most appropriate next management?

options.A: No sentinel lymph node biopsy is needed because the thickness is under 2 mm, and complete excision with a 0.5 cm margin
options.B: Consider sentinel lymph node biopsy (thickness greater than 1.0 mm) and complete the excision with a 1 cm clinical margin
options.C: Offer sentinel lymph node biopsy only if ulceration is present, and excise with a 2 cm margin
options.D: Neither sentinel lymph node biopsy nor wider excision is required because this is stage IA disease
options.E: Stage with whole-body and brain CT before any further surgery because nodal staging is mandatory

questions.explanation: NICE NG14 says not to offer imaging or sentinel lymph node biopsy (SLNB) to people with stage IA melanoma, to consider SLNB when Breslow thickness is 0.8-1.0 mm with at least one adverse feature (ulceration, lymphovascular invasion or mitotic index of 2 or more), and to consider SLNB when thickness is greater than 1.0 mm - so this 1.4 mm melanoma is a candidate for SLNB. Excision margins are 0.5 cm for stage 0, 1 cm for stage I melanoma and 2 cm for stage II, measured around the histological biopsy scar; a 1.4 mm non-ulcerated melanoma is stage I, so a 1 cm margin applies. Whole-body and brain CT is reserved for stage IIB and higher.

references.title: Melanoma: diagnosis and management - recommendations

questions.stem: A 24-year-old man has localised plaque psoriasis affecting the elbows and knees (less than 10% body surface area) with a PASI score of 4. Which of the following is the first-line treatment according to NICE CG153?

options.A: Topical treatment (emollients plus a topical corticosteroid or vitamin D analogue)
options.B: Methotrexate as monotherapy
options.C: Narrowband ultraviolet B phototherapy
options.D: Ciclosporin as monotherapy

questions.explanation: NICE CG153 recommends offering topical treatment as first-line treatment for all people with psoriasis. Second- or third-line options (phototherapy, conventional systemic treatments or targeted immunomodulatory treatments) are offered at the same time only when topical treatment alone is unlikely to control the disease adequately, such as extensive disease (over 10% body surface area or at least moderate on the PASI), or where the impact on quality of life is severe. Methotrexate, phototherapy and ciclosporin are therefore escalations, not initial therapy, for localised plaque psoriasis.

references.title: Psoriasis: assessment and management - recommendations

questions.stem: A 4-year-old girl is brought to clinic with an itchy eruption affecting the elbow flexures, as shown. She has had intermittent flares since infancy. Which of the following statements about her baseline management is correct according to NICE CG57?

image.alt: Atopic dermatitis affecting the flexural crease of the elbow
image.caption: Flexural atopic dermatitis of the elbow crease in a child

options.A: Emollients should be applied only during flares and stopped once the skin clears
options.B: Emollient bath additives should be offered as a first-line addition to standard care
options.C: Topical tacrolimus should be used as first-line treatment for mild eczema of any severity
options.D: Sedating antihistamines should be used routinely to control itch and help sleep
options.E: Emollients are the basis of management and should always be used even when the eczema is clear, and emollient bath additives should not be offered

questions.explanation: NICE CG57 uses a stepped approach in which emollients are the basis of management and should always be used, even when the eczema is clear, with treatment stepped up or down by adding mild, moderate or potent topical corticosteroids (and other options) according to severity. Recommendation 1.5.1.11 states that emollient bath additives should not be offered, because the BATHE trial showed they are not clinically or cost effective (they do not make eczema worse and can be bought over the counter if families wish). Topical calcineurin inhibitors are not first-line treatments, and sedating antihistamines are not recommended routinely for itch.

references.title: Atopic eczema in under 12s: diagnosis and management - recommendations

questions.stem: A 17-year-old boy has moderate-to-severe acne with comedones, inflammatory papules and pustules on the face and upper back. He has already tried simple moisturisers. According to NICE NG198, which of the following is an appropriate first-line treatment option?

options.A: Oral isotretinoin as monotherapy, since all moderate-to-severe acne requires retinoid therapy first
options.B: A topical antibiotic used alone for 6 months to reduce inflammation
options.C: A 12-week course of a fixed combination of topical adapalene with benzoyl peroxide together with oral lymecycline or doxycycline
options.D: Combined oral contraceptive pill as first-line therapy in a male patient
options.E: Benzoyl peroxide alone continued indefinitely without review

questions.explanation: NICE NG198 offers a 12-week course of one of the listed first-line options according to severity. For moderate-to-severe acne these include a fixed combination of topical adapalene with benzoyl peroxide together with either oral lymecycline or oral doxycycline, or topical azelaic acid with an oral antibiotic. Fixed combinations for any severity include adapalene with benzoyl peroxide and tretinoin with clindamycin, while benzoyl peroxide with clindamycin is for mild-to-moderate acne. Antibiotic monotherapy (topical or oral) should not be used alone and courses are reviewed; isotretinoin is reserved for severe acne or where other treatments have failed.

references.title: Acne vulgaris: management - recommendations

questions.stem: An 82-year-old woman is admitted with a displaced intracapsular fracture of the hip after a fall at home. She has correctable comorbidities but they have been treated and no longer delay surgery. According to NICE guidance, when should her surgery be performed?

options.A: Within 6 hours of admission as an emergency case during the night
options.B: On the day of, or the day after, admission, using a planned trauma list
options.C: Within 7 days of admission, once osteoporosis treatment has been started
options.D: Only after an MRI scan has confirmed the fracture in every case
options.E: On day 3 of admission after completion of the physiotherapy assessment

questions.explanation: NICE CG124 recommends performing hip fracture surgery on the day of, or the day after, admission (recommendation 1.2.1) and scheduling it on a planned trauma list (recommendation 1.5.1), which is restated in quality standard QS16. Correctable comorbidities such as anaemia or volume depletion should be identified and treated immediately rather than used to justify delaying surgery. MRI is reserved for suspected occult fractures when plain X-rays of adequate standard are negative.

references.title: Hip fracture: management - recommendations
Hip fracture in adults - quality statements

questions.stem: A 60-year-old woman falls onto an outstretched hand. The radiographs are shown. Which diagnosis best corresponds to the findings?

image.alt: Anteroposterior and lateral wrist radiographs showing a dorsally displaced distal radius fracture with ulnar styloid fracture
image.caption: AP and lateral radiographs demonstrating a dorsally displaced distal radial fracture with ulnar styloid fracture (Colles fracture)
image.source: Wikimedia Commons - File:Collesfracture.jpg (CC BY-SA 3.0, Lucien Monfils)

options.A: Colles fracture - dorsally displaced fracture of the distal radius with ulnar styloid fracture
options.B: Smith fracture - volar displacement of the distal radial fragment
options.C: Barton fracture - fracture-dislocation involving the radiocarpal joint surface
options.D: Galeazzi fracture - distal radius fracture with disruption of the distal radioulnar joint

questions.explanation: The radiographs show a fracture of the distal radius with dorsal displacement of the distal fragment together with an ulnar styloid fracture, which is the classic Colles fracture. NICE NG38 recommends using Bier's block (intravenous regional anaesthesia) to reduce dorsally displaced distal radius fractures in adults, followed by manipulation and plaster or K-wire fixation depending on stability.

references.title: Fractures (non-complex): assessment and management - recommendations

questions.stem: A 24-year-old motorcyclist is brought to the emergency department after a road traffic collision. Examination shows a 3 cm wound over the tibia communicating with a grossly displaced closed fracture; the foot is pale with a capillary refill of 4 seconds. He is haemodynamically stable. Which of the following is the most appropriate immediate action in the emergency department?

options.A: Give intravenous antibiotics only after wound cultures have been obtained in theatre
options.B: Administer intravenous antibiotics immediately, before any further investigation or transfer
options.C: Perform wound excision and delayed primary closure in the emergency department
options.D: Obtain an MRI of the tibia to define soft-tissue injury before starting antibiotics
options.E: Give tetanus prophylaxis alone and start antibiotics only if fever develops

questions.explanation: NICE NG37 recommends giving intravenous antibiotics immediately in the emergency department for patients with an open fracture (recommendation 1.2.22), and pre-hospital antibiotics should be given within 1 hour of injury when available (recommendation 1.1.1). Antibiotics should not wait for cultures, imaging or transfer; wound excision (1.2.28) and fixation with soft-tissue cover within 72 hours (1.2.29) follow as part of the same pathway. Tetanus prophylaxis is given in addition, never instead.

references.title: Open fractures: assessment and management - recommendations
Trauma - quality statements

questions.stem: A 42-year-old man presents with 6 weeks of mechanical low back pain. He has no night pain, fever, weight loss, history of cancer or trauma, and neurological examination is normal. In a non-specialist setting, what is the most appropriate imaging decision?

options.A: Plain radiography of the lumbar spine routinely at the first visit
options.B: Urgent MRI of the lumbar spine to exclude malignancy
options.C: Do not routinely offer imaging; reassess if specific causes or red flags emerge
options.D: CT of the lumbar spine because it involves less radiation than MRI
options.E: Bone scintigraphy to screen for occult metastatic disease

questions.explanation: NICE NG59 recommends that clinicians do not routinely offer imaging for low back pain in a non-specialist setting (recommendation 1.1.4). Assessment should first exclude specific causes such as cancer, infection, trauma and inflammatory conditions (recommendation 1.1.1), with imaging arranged only if these or other red flags are identified.

references.title: Low back pain and sciatica in over 16s: assessment and management - recommendations

questions.stem: A 55-year-old woman immobilised in a below-knee cast after an ankle fracture has no bleeding risk factors and no contraindication to anticoagulation. Her venous thromboembolism risk is judged to outweigh her bleeding risk. According to NICE NG89, which management is recommended?

options.A: No thromboprophylaxis is needed because she can mobilise with crutches
options.B: Aspirin 75 mg daily for the duration of immobilisation as first-line prophylaxis
options.C: Anti-embolism stockings alone, applied over the cast
options.D: Pharmacological prophylaxis with LMWH or fondaparinux, considering stopping it if immobilisation continues beyond 42 days
options.E: Insertion of an inferior vena cava filter before discharge

questions.explanation: NICE NG89 recommends considering pharmacological VTE prophylaxis with LMWH or fondaparinux for people with lower limb immobilisation when the risk of VTE outweighs the risk of bleeding, and considering stopping prophylaxis if immobilisation continues beyond 42 days (recommendation 1.11.1). The decision always requires the individual VTE-versus-bleeding balance (1.1.6), and aspirin is not a recommended option for this scenario.

references.title: Venous thromboembolism in over 16s: reducing the risk of hospital-acquired deep vein thrombosis or pulmonary embolism - recommendations

questions.stem: A 32-year-old man, 8 hours after intramedullary nailing of a tibial diaphyseal fracture, reports pain out of proportion and pain on passive movement of the toes. The calf is tense, distal pulses are palpable, and compartment pressure measures 45 mm Hg with a diastolic pressure of 60 mm Hg. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step?

options.A: Elevate the limb above heart level and observe for 4 hours
options.B: Obtain serial compartment pressure measurements every 6 hours to document the trend
options.C: Start therapeutic heparin for presumed deep vein thrombosis
options.D: Give analgesia and reassess at the next planned ward round
options.E: Perform urgent surgical decompression

questions.explanation: The clinical diagnosis of acute compartment syndrome is supported by pain out of proportion, pain on passive stretch and a tense compartment; BOAST states that once the diagnosis is made, immediate surgical decompression should be carried out. A pressure differential (diastolic minus compartment pressure) below 30 mmHg, as here, or an absolute pressure above 40 mmHg increases the risk and supports urgent fasciotomy rather than watchful waiting. If the diagnosis is genuinely uncertain, circumferential dressings are released and the limb re-evaluated within 30 minutes, but measurement must never delay decompression in a clear case.

references.title: BOAST-10: Compartment syndrome of the limbs
references.org: British Orthopaedic Association Standards for Trauma

questions.topic: Suspected sepsis - risk stratification and antibiotic timing
questions.stem: A 70-year-old man presents with fever and confusion. His NEWS2 score is 8 (respiratory rate 26, SpO2 92% on air, systolic blood pressure 88 mm Hg, heart rate 124, temperature 38.9 °C). Sepsis is suspected. According to NICE NG253, which of the following is correct?

options.A: He is at high risk; give broad-spectrum intravenous antibiotics within 1 hour of the initial assessment
options.B: Antibiotics should be delayed until blood culture results are available
options.C: He is at low risk; start oral antibiotics and review in 24 hours
options.D: Give a 500 mL crystalloid bolus and reassess after 4 hours before considering antibiotics
options.E: Target oxygen saturation of 88-92% because he is at risk of hypercapnic respiratory failure

questions.explanation: NICE NG253 recommends giving broad-spectrum intravenous antibiotics within 1 hour of the initial assessment for people at high risk of sepsis, identified by a NEWS2 score of 7 or more at initial assessment (recommendation 1.8.3), reflecting the guideline's 1-, 3- and 6-hour time limits matched to risk level. Oxygen saturation should be targeted at 94-98% unless there is a risk of hypercapnic respiratory failure (88-92%), and initial fluid boluses are 250 mL. Antibiotics must not wait for culture results.

references.title: Suspected sepsis in people aged 16 or over: recognition, assessment and early management - antibiotic therapy, intravenous fluid and oxygen

questions.stem: A 34-year-old woman with known epilepsy has a generalised tonic-clonic seizure that has lasted 12 minutes despite two doses of intravenous lorazepam given in the emergency department. Which is the most appropriate second-line treatment?

options.A: Intramuscular midazolam 10 mg
options.B: Intravenous phenobarbital 15 mg/kg
options.C: Intravenous levetiracetam, phenytoin or valproate
options.D: A third consecutive dose of intravenous lorazepam before any other drug
options.E: Intranasal midazolam with concurrent intravenous magnesium sulfate

questions.explanation: NICE NG217 gives a benzodiazepine as first-line treatment for status epilepticus (a seizure lasting 5 minutes or longer), and if the seizure has not stopped after the first-line doses, the second-line options are intravenous levetiracetam, phenytoin or valproate (recommendation 7.1.9). Repeated benzodiazepine dosing beyond the recommended two doses risks respiratory depression without replacing second-line therapy.

references.title: Epilepsies in children, young people and adults - 7 Treating status epilepticus, repeated or cluster seizures, and prolonged seizures

questions.stem: A 20-year-old man develops stridor, wheeze and hypotension within minutes of eating a peanut. What is the first-line drug and route?

options.A: Intravenous hydrocortisone 200 mg
options.B: Intramuscular adrenaline into the anterolateral thigh
options.C: Nebulised salbutamol 5 mg
options.D: Intravenous chlorphenamine 10 mg
options.E: Subcutaneous adrenaline into the upper arm

questions.explanation: Resuscitation Council UK's emergency treatment of anaphylaxis guidance gives intramuscular adrenaline into the anterolateral thigh as the first-line treatment, repeated after 5 minutes if there is no improvement. Adjuncts such as corticosteroids, antihistamines and bronchodilators are second-line and never replace adrenaline. The intramuscular thigh route gives the fastest reliable absorption during shock.

references.title: Emergency treatment of anaphylaxis

questions.topic: Diabetic ketoacidosis - fluid and insulin adjustment
questions.stem: A 19-year-old with type 1 diabetes presents with vomiting and Kussmaul breathing: glucose 18 mmol/L, ketones 6.2 mmol/L, pH 7.12, potassium 5.3 mmol/L. He is started on 0.9% saline and a fixed-rate intravenous insulin infusion of 0.1 units/kg/hour. One hour later his glucose has fallen to 9 mmol/L but ketones remain at 6.0 mmol/L. According to JBDS-IP guidance, what is the most appropriate next step?

options.A: Stop the insulin infusion because euglycaemia has been achieved
options.B: Give an intravenous insulin bolus of 10 units
options.C: Switch to intramuscular insulin and continue 0.9% saline only
options.D: Add 10% glucose 125 mL/hour and reduce the fixed-rate insulin to 0.05 units/kg/hour
options.E: Commence continuous renal replacement therapy for the acidosis

questions.explanation: JBDS-IP guidance states that when the glycaemic target (14 mmol/L or below) is reached while ketonaemia persists, 10% glucose 125 mL/hour should be added and the fixed-rate insulin reduced to 0.05 units/kg/hour, maintaining a ketone fall of at least 0.5 mmol/L/hour. Simply stopping insulin would halt ketone clearance, and a bolus is not indicated. Potassium of 5.3 mmol/L means no potassium is added to the first litre at this stage.

references.title: Guidelines for the management of diabetic ketoacidosis in adults

questions.stem: A 64-year-old man with chronic kidney disease has a serum potassium of 6.8 mmol/L with peaked T waves on ECG. Which drug should be given first?

options.A: Intravenous calcium gluconate 10% to stabilise the myocardium
options.B: Intravenous insulin with glucose to shift potassium into cells
options.C: Nebulised salbutamol 12.5 g
options.D: Oral sodium zirconium cyclosilicate

questions.explanation: UK Kidney Association guidance gives intravenous calcium gluconate 30 mL of 10% (or calcium chloride 10 mL of 10%) for severe hyperkalaemia with potassium of 6.5 mmol/L or above, particularly with ECG changes; it stabilises the myocardium without lowering potassium. Insulin with glucose and high-dose nebulised salbutamol then shift potassium intracellularly, and elimination strategies follow. Oral binders act too slowly for emergency stabilisation.

references.title: Clinical practice guideline for hyperkalaemia - Section II: Hospital

questions.topic: Major trauma - rapid sequence intubation timing
questions.stem: A patient with major trauma requires drug-assisted rapid sequence intubation in the emergency department. According to NICE quality standard QS166, within what time frame of the initial call should this be performed?

options.A: Within 15 minutes
options.B: Within 30 minutes
options.C: Within 45 minutes
options.D: Within 60 minutes
options.E: Within 90 minutes

questions.explanation: NICE QS166 (Trauma) specifies that people needing drug-assisted rapid sequence intubation receive it within 45 minutes of the initial call as part of airway management in major trauma. The same quality standard requires open fracture fixation with definitive soft-tissue cover within 72 hours of injury when this is not performed at the time of wound excision.

references.title: Trauma - quality statements

questions.topic: Mental Capacity Act - assessment of capacity
questions.stem: A 67-year-old man with moderate dementia refuses a recommended hip replacement, saying he prefers to live with the pain. His MMSE is 18/30. His daughter argues that he must lack capacity because he has dementia. Which statement about the assessment of capacity is correct?

options.A: Capacity is absent automatically once a diagnosis of dementia is made
options.B: Capacity is a permanent global trait, so one assessment applies to all future decisions
options.C: Capacity is decision-specific and time-specific, and an unwise decision does not itself prove incapacity
options.D: Only a psychiatrist may assess capacity, and best interests determine whether capacity is present
options.E: The daughter, as next of kin, must consent whenever the patient refuses treatment

questions.explanation: Under section 3 of the Mental Capacity Act 2005, a person is unable to make a decision if they cannot understand, retain, use or weigh the relevant information, or communicate the decision, and the OPG guidance requires the assessment to be specific to the particular decision at the particular time. A diagnosis such as dementia does not by itself remove capacity, and an unwise or eccentric decision is not evidence of incapacity (principle 3). Where incapacity is established, treatment decisions are then made in the person's best interests.

references.title: Mental Capacity Act 2005, section 3: inability to make decisions
Making decisions: a guide for people who work in health and social care
references.org: GOV.UK / Office of the Public Guardian

questions.stem: An 80-year-old man with advanced heart failure asks his cardiologist to record a 'do not attempt cardiopulmonary resuscitation' decision in his notes. Which statement is correct?

options.A: The patient has the legal right to demand CPR, so the doctor must comply
options.B: The decision is made by a doctor, applies only to CPR, and the patient should be involved and informed unless this would cause harm
options.C: The patient's written consent is a legal requirement for a valid DNACPR decision
options.D: The decision automatically applies to all other treatments, including antibiotics and intravenous fluids
options.E: Any trained healthcare assistant may record the decision after a family meeting

questions.explanation: NHS guidance states that the DNACPR decision is made by a doctor (or other trained, competent clinician) after discussion, and that a patient cannot demand CPR that would be futile, although they may seek a second opinion. The decision covers cardiopulmonary resuscitation only, not other treatments, and formal consent is not required, but the patient must be involved and informed unless being told would cause them harm. Decisions are individual and never applied as blanket policies.

references.title: Do not attempt cardiopulmonary resuscitation (DNACPR) decisions

questions.stem: In a study of a new screening test, 90 of 100 people with the disease test positive and 10 test negative; among 100 people without the disease, 80 test negative and 20 test positive. What is the sensitivity of the test?
questions.explanation: Sensitivity is the proportion of diseased people who test positive: true positives divided by (true positives + false negatives) = 90/100 = 90%. Specificity here is 80% (option B), the positive predictive value is 90/110, about 82% (option C), and overall accuracy is 170/200 = 85% (option D).

references.title: Diagnostic tests 1: sensitivity and specificity

questions.stem: A new diagnostic test has a sensitivity of 90% and a specificity of 80%. What is its positive likelihood ratio?
questions.explanation: The positive likelihood ratio is sensitivity divided by (1 - specificity): 0.90 / (1 - 0.80) = 4.5. The negative likelihood ratio would be (1 - 0.90) / 0.80 = 0.125 (option A). A positive likelihood ratio above 10 is generally regarded as generating a large and often conclusive shift in probability.

references.title: Diagnostic tests 4: likelihood ratios

questions.stem: A 29-year-old woman in labour is advised to have an emergency caesarean section. She asks what would have happened if she had been told about a small risk of a serious complication and had declined. Under the Montgomery ruling, when is a doctor negligent for failing to disclose a risk?

options.A: Only when the risk exceeds 1 in 100, as set by a fixed numerical threshold
options.B: When a responsible body of doctors would not have disclosed it (the professional standard)
options.C: Only when the undisclosed risk actually materialised and caused harm
options.D: When a reasonable person in the patient's position would be likely to attach significance to the risk and the patient would have chosen differently
options.E: When the patient has signed a blanket consent form accepting all risks

questions.explanation: In Montgomery v Lanarkshire Health Board [2015] UKSC 11 the Supreme Court held that doctors must take reasonable care to ensure patients are aware of material risks involved in recommended treatment and of reasonable alternatives, replacing the professional-standard approach with a patient-centred test. A risk is material if a reasonable person in the patient's position would be likely to attach significance to it. There is no fixed numerical threshold, and GMC consent guidance restates this duty.

references.title: Montgomery v Lanarkshire Health Board [2015] UKSC 11
references.org: UK Supreme Court / Find Case Law

references.title: Consent: patients and doctors making decisions together

questions.stem: The photomicrograph shows myocardium obtained several days after coronary artery occlusion. Which pathological process is demonstrated?

image.alt: Histopathology of myocardium showing cardiomyocytes with hypereosinophilic cytoplasm
image.caption: Coagulative necrosis of cardiomyocytes with cytoplasmic hypereosinophilia after ischaemic injury
image.source: Wikimedia Commons - File:Histopathology of coagulative necrosis of cardiomyocytes.jpg (CC BY 3.0, Katarzyna Michaud et al.)

options.A: Coagulative necrosis with preserved cell outlines and eosinophilic cytoplasm
options.B: Caseous necrosis with granular debris and a rim of epithelioid cells
options.C: Liquefactive necrosis with complete loss of architecture and pus formation
options.D: Fat necrosis with shadowy cell outlines and calcium soap formation

questions.explanation: Ischaemic injury to the heart produces coagulative necrosis: the cytoplasm becomes intensely eosinophilic while the basic cell outlines are preserved in the early stages, with nuclei undergoing pyknosis, karyorrhexis and karyolysis. Caseous necrosis is typical of tuberculosis, liquefactive necrosis of brain infarcts and bacterial abscesses, and fat necrosis of acute pancreatitis or trauma to fat.

questions.stem: In the current (2022) formulation of the hallmarks of cancer, which of the following is classified as an enabling characteristic that facilitates the acquisition of hallmark capabilities, rather than a hallmark capability itself?

options.A: Sustaining proliferative signalling
options.B: Avoiding immune destruction
options.C: Tumour-promoting inflammation
options.D: Inducing angiogenesis
options.E: Activating invasion and metastasis

questions.explanation: The 2022 depiction comprises eight hallmark capabilities (the original six, now including reprogramming cellular metabolism and avoiding immune destruction) plus two enabling characteristics: genome instability and mutation, and tumour-promoting inflammation. The 2022 review also proposed emerging dimensions of unlocking phenotypic plasticity, non-mutational epigenetic reprogramming, polymorphic microbiomes and senescent cells. Options A, B, D and E are all hallmark capabilities, not enabling characteristics.

references.title: Hallmarks of Cancer: New Dimensions
Biological Hallmarks of Cancer

questions.topic: Coagulation screening tests - factor VII deficiency
questions.stem: A 22-year-old man presents with recurrent bleeding after dental extraction. His full blood count and platelet count are normal, the prothrombin time is prolonged, the activated partial thromboplastin time is normal, and mixing studies correct the prothrombin time. Which factor deficiency explains these findings?

options.A: Factor VIII
options.B: Factor IX
options.C: Factor XI
options.D: Factor XIII
options.E: Factor VII

questions.explanation: The prothrombin time tests the extrinsic pathway (factors I, II, V, VII and X) while the activated partial thromboplastin time tests the intrinsic pathway (factors I, II, V, VIII, IX, XI and XII), so an isolated prolonged PT with a normal aPTT localises the defect to the extrinsic limb - most often factor VII deficiency, which also corrects on mixing. Platelet counts are unaffected. Factor XIII deficiency would give normal screening tests, and factors VIII, IX or XI would prolong the aPTT.

questions.stem: A patient with epilepsy is started on phenytoin. After several days of dosing, each small dose increase produces a disproportionately large rise in the serum concentration, and the apparent half-lengthens as the dose rises. Which of the following best explains this observation?

options.A: Phenytoin induces its own metabolism, so concentrations fall with continued dosing
options.B: Phenytoin follows zero-order kinetics because its metabolic enzymes become saturated, so a constant amount is eliminated per unit time
options.C: Phenytoin has an extremely small volume of distribution, confining it to the plasma compartment
options.D: Protein binding increases at higher doses, trapping more drug in plasma
options.E: Phenytoin is excreted unchanged by the kidneys in direct proportion to dose

questions.explanation: At therapeutic concentrations the enzymes metabolising phenytoin become saturated, so the drug follows zero-order (saturation) kinetics: a constant amount rather than a constant fraction is eliminated per unit time, so small dose increments cause disproportionately large rises in concentration and the half-life lengthens as concentration rises. This contrasts with first-order kinetics, where the half-life is constant. Phenytoin has a large volume of distribution influenced by lipophilicity and protein binding, which is why loading doses are calculated from volume of distribution rather than clearance.

references.title: Pharmacokinetic characteristics of antiepileptic drugs (AEDs)

questions.stem: A drug has a volume of distribution of 20 L/kg of body weight. Which statement about this drug is correct?

options.A: The drug is largely confined to the plasma compartment
options.B: The drug is extensively distributed into body tissues, and a loading dose may be needed to reach therapeutic concentrations quickly
options.C: Its clearance from the body is necessarily reduced
options.D: It can only be given as a continuous intravenous infusion

questions.explanation: Volume of distribution is the apparent volume into which the drug distributes (amount in the body divided by plasma concentration); a value of 20 L/kg, far above plasma volume of about 0.07 L/kg, indicates extensive uptake into tissues, influenced by lipophilicity and protein binding. A loading dose calculated as target concentration multiplied by weight and volume of distribution can achieve therapeutic levels rapidly when the volume of distribution is large. Clearance and route of administration are independent of volume of distribution.

references.title: Pharmacokinetic characteristics of antiepileptic drugs (AEDs)

questions.stem: A patient with meticillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus bacteraemia is started on daptomycin. Which statement about daptomycin is correct?

options.A: It inhibits cell-wall synthesis by binding penicillin-binding proteins
options.B: It binds the 50S ribosomal subunit and prevents translocation
options.C: It inhibits nucleic acid synthesis and is active against Gram-negative bacilli
options.D: It binds phosphatidylglycerol in a calcium-dependent manner to depolarise the cytoplasmic membrane of Gram-positive bacteria, and it is inactivated by pulmonary surfactant
options.E: It blocks folate synthesis and is used for uncomplicated urinary tract infection

questions.explanation: Daptomycin is a cyclic lipopeptide whose insertion into the cytoplasmic membrane of Gram-positive bacteria requires calcium and depends on binding to membrane phosphatidylglycerol, causing rapid depolarisation and cell death. Because pulmonary surfactant inactivates it, daptomycin is not used to treat pneumonia despite its Gram-positive activity. Options A, B, C and E describe beta-lactams, macrolides, fluoroquinolones/nitroimidazoles and trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole respectively.

references.title: More Than a Pore: A Current Perspective on the In Vivo Mode of Action of the Lipopeptide Antibiotic Daptomycin

questions.stem: In the Spaulding classification used to guide disinfection and sterilisation of patient-care items, which pairing is correct?

options.A: Critical items - low-level disinfection
options.B: Semicritical items - sterilisation is mandatory in every case
options.C: Semicritical items such as laryngoscope blades - high-level disinfection
options.D: Noncritical items such as blood pressure cuffs - sterilisation
options.E: Semicritical items - low-level disinfection is sufficient

questions.explanation: The CDC's rational approach classifies items by infection risk: critical items (entering sterile tissue or the vascular system) must be sterile, semicritical items (contacting mucous membranes or non-intact skin, such as laryngoscope blades) require at least high-level disinfection, and noncritical items contacting intact skin (such as blood pressure cuffs) require cleaning and low-level disinfection. High-level disinfection eliminates all microorganisms except small numbers of bacterial spores.

references.title: A rational approach to disinfection and sterilization (Guideline for Disinfection and Sterilization in Healthcare Facilities)

options.A: Escherichia coli

options.D: Pseudomonas aeruginosa

questions.stem: Which of the following pathogens belongs to the critical priority group of the WHO Bacterial Priority Pathogens List 2024?

options.A: Carbapenem-resistant Acinetobacter baumannii
options.B: Carbapenem-resistant Pseudomonas aeruginosa
options.C: Meticillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus
options.D: Vancomycin-resistant Enterococcus faecium
options.E: Fluoroquinolone-resistant Salmonella Typhi

questions.explanation: The WHO Bacterial Priority Pathogens List 2024 places carbapenem-resistant Acinetobacter baumannii, carbapenem-resistant Enterobacterales, third-generation cephalosporin-resistant Enterobacterales and rifampicin-resistant Mycobacterium tuberculosis in the critical priority group. Carbapenem-resistant Pseudomonas aeruginosa, meticillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus, vancomycin-resistant Enterococcus faecium and fluoroquinolone-resistant Salmonella Typhi are in the high priority group. The list covers 24 pathogens across 15 families to guide research, development and public-health action against antimicrobial resistance.
